# digital nomads

## live, work, and explore in costa rica

Costa Rica’s digital nomad program invites international residents to work remotely from the land of pura vida. This program extends a 90-day tourist visa to a full year, with the option to renew for an additional year. Digital nomads are exempt from income tax and enjoy other benefits including the ability to open a national bank account in Costa Rica and validation of their home country’s driver’s license. Digital nomads may also waive customs taxes on telecommunications and electronic devices necessary to fulfill remote work requirements (conditions apply).

## work remote from costa rica

Find your balance as you work remotely from Costa Rica. You can now extend a 90-day tourist visa to experience a full year (or longer) in Costa Rica. Applications must show proof of a stable net income of at least $3,000 per month ($5,000 for families). Mandatory medical insurance must cover you through the length of your stay, and the digital nomad visa requires a one-time fee.

## FAQs

### The regulation states that all of the required documents in the application have to be translated into Spanish. Who is able to provide such a translation?

To be on the safe side, applicants can have the translation completed by an official translator registered with the Costa Rican Ministry of Foreign Affairs, or a notary public with knowledge of the language.

Documents can also be translated abroad, but the official sources consulted note that working with a Costa Rican translator is more practical, as this can prevent errors or problems with translations done in applicants’ home countries, which generally slow down the process.

### Where do digital nomads have to make the $100 deposit (receipt of payment to the Government) required to enter the country?

**Proof of payment to the Government in the amount of one hundred dollars (US$100.00) or its equivalent in colones at the reference exchange rate of the Central Bank of Costa Rica, in accordance with Article 256 of the General Law of Migration and Foreigners. This deposit must be made to account number 001-0242480-0 of the Bank of Costa Rica, with the IBAN account number CR15015201001024248003.**

**Dear user:** If you are making the payment via international bank transfer, please take the following information into account**BEFORE** making your payment:

**Applicant Information:** Make one transfer per applicant. In the case of dependent persons, the payment must be made in the name of each individual applicant.

The following information must be included:

*   Name of the bank
*   SWIFT code
*   ABA code (only for banks in the United States)  
You can find this information in the list of Banco de Costa Rica Correspondent Banks at the following link:  
[https://bancobcr.com/wps/portal/bcr/bancobcr/empresas/bcr_comercio_exterior/productos_y_servicios/bancos_corresponsales_directos/](https://bancobcr.com/wps/portal/bcr/bancobcr/empresas/bcr_comercio_exterior/productos_y_servicios/bancos_corresponsales_directos/)

**Full name of the beneficiary:** ESTADO MINISTERIO DE HACIENDA  
**Full IBAN account name (International Bank Account Number):** CR15015201001024248003  
**Address:** San José, Calle 03 Avenida 02, Ministry of Finance, former Anglo Bank building

**Also, provide the information of the Bank of Costa Rica, which receives the funds:**

*   **Name of the Bank:** Banco de Costa Rica
*   **Address:** Central and Second Avenues, between 4th and 6th Streets, San José, Costa Rica
*   **SWIFT Code:** BCRICRSJ
*   **UID (Universal ID):** 019339

**Important Information:**  
The $100 fee related to this application must be**received in full (net)** by the Ministry of Finance accounts. Therefore, it is important to consider bank fees—**both from the sending bank abroad and from the receiving bank (Banco de Costa Rica), which charges a fee of $15.**

### How does the medical services insurance work for digital nomads?

The medical services insurance must cover the full duration of the digital nomad’s stay in Costa Rica for the full period authorized, and must have a coverage of at least USD $50,000.

The policy may be from an international provider or a Costa Rican insurance firm regulated by the Office of the Superintendent General for Insurance of Costa Rica. Any dependents accompanying the digital nomad to Costa Rica must also be covered by an insurance policy.

### What requirements does a digital nomad need to meet to open a bank account with a Costa Rican financial institution?

Digital nomads may open savings accounts in financial institutions belonging to the national banking system provided that they comply with the provisions of the Law on Narcotics, Psychotropic Substances, Unauthorized Drugs, Connected Activities, Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing (8.204).

They must also comply with all regulatory frameworks relating to the fight against money laundering. The Office of the Superintendent General of Financial Institutions (SUGEF) will issue any regulations or guidelines that prove necessary.

### Do I need legal assitance to apply?

No, no legal assistance is required.

# digital nomads

## live, work, and explore in costa rica

Costa Rica’s digital nomad program invites international residents to work remotely from the land of pura vida. This program extends a 90-day tourist visa to a full year, with the option to renew for an additional year. Digital nomads are exempt from income tax and enjoy other benefits including the ability to open a national bank account in Costa Rica and validation of their home country’s driver’s license. Digital nomads may also waive customs taxes on telecommunications and electronic devices necessary to fulfill remote work requirements (conditions apply).

## work remote from costa rica

Find your balance as you work remotely from Costa Rica. You can now extend a 90-day tourist visa to experience a full year (or longer) in Costa Rica. Applications must show proof of a stable net income of at least $3,000 per month ($5,000 for families). Mandatory medical insurance must cover you through the length of your stay, and the digital nomad visa requires a one-time fee.

## FAQs

### The regulation states that all of the required documents in the application have to be translated into Spanish. Who is able to provide such a translation?

To be on the safe side, applicants can have the translation completed by an official translator registered with the Costa Rican Ministry of Foreign Affairs, or a notary public with knowledge of the language.

Documents can also be translated abroad, but the official sources consulted note that working with a Costa Rican translator is more practical, as this can prevent errors or problems with translations done in applicants’ home countries, which generally slow down the process.

### Where do digital nomads have to make the $100 deposit (receipt of payment to the Government) required to enter the country?

**Proof of payment to the Government in the amount of one hundred dollars (US$100.00) or its equivalent in colones at the reference exchange rate of the Central Bank of Costa Rica, in accordance with Article 256 of the General Law of Migration and Foreigners. This deposit must be made to account number 001-0242480-0 of the Bank of Costa Rica, with the IBAN account number CR15015201001024248003.**

**Dear user:** If you are making the payment via international bank transfer, please take the following information into account**BEFORE** making your payment:

**Applicant Information:** Make one transfer per applicant. In the case of dependent persons, the payment must be made in the name of each individual applicant.

The following information must be included:

*   Name of the bank
*   SWIFT code
*   ABA code (only for banks in the United States)  
You can find this information in the list of Banco de Costa Rica Correspondent Banks at the following link:  
[https://bancobcr.com/wps/portal/bcr/bancobcr/empresas/bcr_comercio_exterior/productos_y_servicios/bancos_corresponsales_directos/](https://bancobcr.com/wps/portal/bcr/bancobcr/empresas/bcr_comercio_exterior/productos_y_servicios/bancos_corresponsales_directos/)

**Full name of the beneficiary:** ESTADO MINISTERIO DE HACIENDA  
**Full IBAN account name (International Bank Account Number):** CR15015201001024248003  
**Address:** San José, Calle 03 Avenida 02, Ministry of Finance, former Anglo Bank building

**Also, provide the information of the Bank of Costa Rica, which receives the funds:**

*   **Name of the Bank:** Banco de Costa Rica
*   **Address:** Central and Second Avenues, between 4th and 6th Streets, San José, Costa Rica
*   **SWIFT Code:** BCRICRSJ
*   **UID (Universal ID):** 019339

**Important Information:**  
The $100 fee related to this application must be**received in full (net)** by the Ministry of Finance accounts. Therefore, it is important to consider bank fees—**both from the sending bank abroad and from the receiving bank (Banco de Costa Rica), which charges a fee of $15.**

### How does the medical services insurance work for digital nomads?

The medical services insurance must cover the full duration of the digital nomad’s stay in Costa Rica for the full period authorized, and must have a coverage of at least USD $50,000.

The policy may be from an international provider or a Costa Rican insurance firm regulated by the Office of the Superintendent General for Insurance of Costa Rica. Any dependents accompanying the digital nomad to Costa Rica must also be covered by an insurance policy.

### What requirements does a digital nomad need to meet to open a bank account with a Costa Rican financial institution?

Digital nomads may open savings accounts in financial institutions belonging to the national banking system provided that they comply with the provisions of the Law on Narcotics, Psychotropic Substances, Unauthorized Drugs, Connected Activities, Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing (8.204).

They must also comply with all regulatory frameworks relating to the fight against money laundering. The Office of the Superintendent General of Financial Institutions (SUGEF) will issue any regulations or guidelines that prove necessary.

### Do I need legal assitance to apply?

No, no legal assistance is required.

A growing wave of [digital nomads](https://www.rippling.com/glossary/digital-nomad) is discovering that Colombia offers a dynamic environment for remote work. From the bustling streets of Bogotá to the entrepreneurial vibes of Medellín and the scenic charm of coastal towns like Cartagena, Colombia offers many prime destinations for foreign expats seeking adventure, culture, and cost-effective living. It also offers an official digital nomad visa designed specifically for foreigners who want to work remotely in the country.

Whether you're a seasoned digital nomad or someone exploring a new place to set up your laptop, the Colombian government's program might be exactly what you need to enjoy all the unique experiences this fascinating country has to offer — without quitting your day job.

In this article, you'll learn what the Colombia digital nomad visa entails, who's eligible, how to start the visa application process, and the specific documents you'll need to submit to immigration authorities. We'll also cover the benefits of living as a digital nomad in Colombia, the main differences between this visa and a tourist visa, and answer some common questions about taxes and more.

## Does Colombia offer a digital nomad visa?

Yes. Colombia offers a special digital nomad visa — officially the Visa V – Nómadas Digitales, under Resolución 5477 de 2022 — for foreign professionals, [remote workers](https://www.rippling.com/blog/managing-remote-teams), and freelancers who want to work remotely in the country without seeking local employment. The primary objective is to attract digital nomads and entrepreneurs who can bring economic activity to Colombia and contribute to its thriving international community of expats.

This Colombian visa differs from a traditional work permit because it specifically targets individuals who earn their income from foreign sources. Instead of requiring a local employment contract, the digital nomad visa permits you to continue working for your clients or employers abroad while you enjoy everything Colombia has to offer. For many digital nomads, this is a more convenient route than something like an investment visa, as it aligns better with their remote working lifestyle and doesn't necessarily require large amounts of capital.

## 4 benefits of a Colombia digital nomad visa

### 1. Extended stay

With a Colombia digital nomad visa, foreigners can stay in Colombia for a longer duration than typically allowed by a tourist visa. This means you can settle into a favorite neighborhood in Medellín or Bogotá — perhaps El Poblado, a popular choice for young expats in Colombia — where you can build connections and fully experience the daily life that makes this country so appealing to international expats.

### 2. Work legally

Unlike a tourist visa, a digital nomad visa in Colombia offers the legal framework to carry out remote work for [foreign clients or companies](https://www.rippling.com/blog/work-remotely-for-a-us-company). This is a significant advantage over the typical restrictions you might face if you simply visited Colombia on a tourist visa, which wouldn't allow you to engage in work of any kind.

### 3. Cost-effective living

Many international digital nomads find Colombia to be an affordable destination. Daily expenses, from rent to dining, can be significantly lower than in other countries, making it easier to thrive on modest incomes. Whether you prefer the energetic vibe of Bogotá or the laid-back lifestyle of Caribbean coastal towns, you'll likely find a range of budget-friendly options.

### 4. Networking opportunities

The influx of foreign remote workers and freelancers to Colombia has resulted in a rapidly expanding tech and coworking scene. Whether in Medellín or Bogotá, you'll discover numerous coworking spaces, regular meetups, and conferences that are perfect for forging new professional connections. It's easy to meet like-minded digital nomads, entrepreneurs, and expats who can help you explore innovative ideas or collaborate on new projects.

## Advantages of living in Colombia as a digital nomad

There are many reasons why digital nomads are choosing Colombia as a work destination. Here are a few of the most common ones:

*   **Affordable cost of living:**From groceries to rent, many major cities in Colombia can be easier on your wallet than comparable destinations in other countries.

*   **Warm climate and natural beauty:**Whether you love the spring-like weather of Medellín, the cosmopolitan charm of Bogotá, or the coastal allure of Cartagena, there's a climate and scenic backdrop for just about everyone.

*   **Accessible travel options:**Traveling to Colombia has become simpler thanks to multiple international flights and well-connected domestic airlines. It's also a great jumping-off point for visiting neighboring countries in Latin America.

*   **Fast-growing digital nomad community:**The trend of the Medellín digital nomad is real — the expat community in Colombia is thriving. You'll encounter coworking hubs and cafés bustling with remote workers from all over the world.

## Colombia digital nomad visa eligibility

To qualify for a Colombia digital nomad visa, the applicant must have a valid passport from a country exempt from needing a short-stay visa in Colombia. Those countries include (but are not limited to):

*   United States

*   Germany

*   Australia

*   Canada

*   Spain

*   Indonesia

*   Portugal

Applicants also typically need to fit into one of the following categories:

*   [Remote workers or freelancers](https://www.rippling.com/blog/telework-vs-remote-work) working with foreign companies or clients.

*   Entrepreneurs with digital-focused businesses who want to operate in Colombia but do not plan to engage in local employment.

In many cases, immigration authorities will want to confirm that your source of income comes from abroad rather than from a Colombian employer.

## Colombia digital nomad visa requirements

If you're gearing up for a Colombia digital nomad visa, here are some main requirements to keep in mind:

*   **Proof of remote work or freelancing for at least six months:**This may include client contracts, reference letters, or an official letter in Spanish or English describing your remote work arrangement. If you're an entrepreneur, you can submit a motivational letter explaining your work and how it will support your lifestyle in Colombia.

*   **A valid passport:**Make sure your passport is current for the duration of your planned stay, with at least six months of remaining validity.

*   **Passport-style photo** with a white background, taken within the last six months.

*   **Minimum income:**Applicants must show monthly income of at least three times Colombia's minimum monthly wage (SMMLV). As of 2026, that threshold is roughly $1,100–$1,400 USD per month, depending on the exchange rate the Colombian Ministry of Foreign Affairs applies when reviewing your file. Each of the last several months must individually meet the threshold — averaging your income across months isn't accepted, so build in a buffer above the minimum.

*   **Health insurance covering Colombia:**Your policy must explicitly include medical repatriation coverage for the full duration of your stay. General travel insurance typically doesn't qualify; it needs to be a health insurance policy.

*   **Proof of your relationship to any dependents**, if applicable.

Visa requirements can change, so always double-check the latest details from the Colombian consulate or the Cancillería's official immigration website to make sure you have the most up-to-date information.

## Colombia digital nomad visa application

Below is a step-by-step look at how to begin your visa application for the Colombia digital nomad visa. Generally, you'll have to submit all required documents through an online portal or at a Colombian consulate abroad.

### Step 1: Check eligibility

Before you invest time in collecting documents, verify that you meet the basic criteria: Are you a digital nomad working with foreign clients or companies? Can you demonstrate the required income?

### Step 2: Prepare the required documents

Compile your passport, bank statements (the only accepted proof of income — invoices and tax returns alone typically aren't sufficient), insurance policy details with explicit repatriation coverage, and proof of remote work. You might need a formal letter in Spanish explaining your remote work arrangement and how you meet the minimum income threshold.

### Step 3: Submit your application

Start your [online visa application](https://tramitesmre.cancilleria.gov.co/tramites/enlinea/solicitarVisa.xhtml), which can be found on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' online portal. Alternatively, you can visit your nearest Colombian consulate to apply. Be meticulous about uploading the correct documents — missing even a single required file can delay the process.

### Step 4: Pay the application fee

A visa study fee is required to move your application forward, generally around $54 USD. The exact amount can vary depending on the exchange rate between Colombian pesos and USD at the time you apply. Keep in mind there may be additional charges if you're submitting from a consulate abroad.

### Step 5: Wait for approval

Processing times typically run up to 30 calendar days, though they can vary based on application volume and how complete your documentation is. The immigration authorities will review your visa application and notify you of any additional documents needed.

### Step 6: Receive your visa and pay visa fees

Once approved, you'll need to pay an issuance fee before receiving your visa, generally in the $170–$230 USD range depending on exchange rates at the time. Once you've paid, you'll get your Colombia digital nomad visa electronically or via a stamp in your passport. If your visa is valid for more than three months, you'll also need to register with Migración Colombia and obtain a Cédula de Extranjería within 15 days of arrival. From there, you're permitted to live and work remotely in Colombia under the specific terms outlined by the visa.

## Colombia digital nomad visa restrictions

While Colombia's digital nomad visa offers [flexibility to remote workers](https://www.rippling.com/blog/remote-work-software), there are some key restrictions:

### Employment restrictions

You cannot take up local employment with a Colombian company or provide services to Colombian clients, as the digital nomad visa is designed strictly for foreign remote workers who provide services to clients abroad.

### Length of stay

The digital nomad visa allows stays of up to two years, at the discretion of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Time on this visa does not count toward permanent residency. Keep in mind, too, that exceeding the allowed time may lead to penalties or future immigration complications.

### Income requirements

You'll have to maintain the minimum income threshold (three times the SMMLV, roughly $1,100–$1,400 USD/month as of 2026) throughout your stay, with each month individually meeting the bar. Falling below the threshold in any given month could jeopardize your visa status.

### Travel restrictions

While traveling to Colombia is relatively simple, your visa is generally cancelled if you're absent from the country for more than six consecutive months. Check the latest official guidelines to confirm current rules around exits and re-entries on a digital nomad visa.

### Compliance and obligations

Maintaining valid health insurance with repatriation coverage, continuing to meet the income requirements every month, and avoiding unauthorized activities (like taking on local jobs or clients) are part of your obligations as a digital nomad under this visa. Once you cross 183 days in Colombia within any rolling 12-month period, you also become a Colombian tax resident, which means declaring worldwide income — so plan ahead with a tax professional if that threshold applies to you.

## Colombia digital nomad visa vs. tourist visa

While both a tourist visa and a digital nomad visa allow foreigners to stay in Colombia, each serves a distinct purpose and there are key differences between them:

*   **Duration of stay:**A tourist visa generally offers a shorter duration — generally up to 180 days — while the digital nomad visa can allow you to stay for up to two years.

*   **Activities permitted:**On a tourist visa, you're typically not legally allowed to work remotely for extended periods. The digital nomad visa, on the other hand, explicitly permits you to engage in remote work for foreign entities.

*   **Income verification:**A tourist visa does not require you to prove a monthly income, whereas the digital nomad visa does, and requires it every month without averaging.

## Colombia digital nomad visa FAQs

Do digital nomads pay tax in Colombia?

Tax rules can be complex. Digital nomads who spend more than half of the tax year in Colombia may be considered tax residents, depending on specific income and immigration factors. Consult a local tax professional to make sure you’re fully compliant.

How long does it take to get a digital nomad visa in Colombia?

Processing times vary, but most applicants can expect a timeframe of one to three weeks once they’ve submitted all proper documents and paid the necessary application fee and visa fee.

What is the easiest country to get a digital nomad visa?

It can differ based on your personal situation and income level. Besides Colombia, many other countries in Latin America, Europe, and Asia also provide digital nomad visas—and these types of visas are becoming more and more common as countries strive to attract remote workers who can stimulate their economies without taking away local jobs. There are pros and cons in each country, however, and your preference might depend on factors like cost of living, community, climate, and how smoothly the local authorities handle visa applications.

How much income do I need to qualify for Colombia's digital nomad visa?

You need to show monthly income equal to at least three times Colombia's minimum monthly wage (SMMLV). As of 2026, that works out to roughly $1,100–$1,400 USD per month, depending on the exchange rate used when your application is reviewed. Each of your last several months of income statements must individually meet the threshold; averaging is not accepted, so it's wise to apply with a buffer above the minimum.

Can I bring my family on a Colombia digital nomad visa?

Yes. Dependents — such as a spouse or children — can typically be included on your application if you provide proof of the relationship, like a marriage or birth certificate. Each dependent generally needs their own supporting documentation, and consulates may ask for additional proof that you can financially support them during your stay.

Can I work for a Colombian company while on a digital nomad visa?

No. The digital nomad visa is strictly for remote work performed for foreign companies or clients — it doesn't permit local employment or providing services to Colombian clients. If you want to take a job with a Colombian employer, you'll need to apply for a different visa category, such as a work visa sponsored by that employer.

Do I need health insurance for the Colombia digital nomad visa?

Yes, but it must be health insurance with explicit medical repatriation coverage for the full duration of your stay — general travel insurance plans typically don't qualify. Many digital nomads use international or expat-focused health insurance providers that are designed to meet this requirement.

Can I renew my Colombia digital nomad visa?

Colombia's digital nomad visa is valid for up to two years, and renewal is possible, though time on this visa does not count toward permanent residency. To renew, you'll generally need to reapply with updated proof of income, health insurance, and remote work status, following the same process as your original application.

A growing wave of [digital nomads](https://www.rippling.com/glossary/digital-nomad) is discovering that Colombia offers a dynamic environment for remote work. From the bustling streets of Bogotá to the entrepreneurial vibes of Medellín and the scenic charm of coastal towns like Cartagena, Colombia offers many prime destinations for foreign expats seeking adventure, culture, and cost-effective living. It also offers an official digital nomad visa designed specifically for foreigners who want to work remotely in the country.

Whether you're a seasoned digital nomad or someone exploring a new place to set up your laptop, the Colombian government's program might be exactly what you need to enjoy all the unique experiences this fascinating country has to offer — without quitting your day job.

In this article, you'll learn what the Colombia digital nomad visa entails, who's eligible, how to start the visa application process, and the specific documents you'll need to submit to immigration authorities. We'll also cover the benefits of living as a digital nomad in Colombia, the main differences between this visa and a tourist visa, and answer some common questions about taxes and more.

## Does Colombia offer a digital nomad visa?

Yes. Colombia offers a special digital nomad visa — officially the Visa V – Nómadas Digitales, under Resolución 5477 de 2022 — for foreign professionals, [remote workers](https://www.rippling.com/blog/managing-remote-teams), and freelancers who want to work remotely in the country without seeking local employment. The primary objective is to attract digital nomads and entrepreneurs who can bring economic activity to Colombia and contribute to its thriving international community of expats.

This Colombian visa differs from a traditional work permit because it specifically targets individuals who earn their income from foreign sources. Instead of requiring a local employment contract, the digital nomad visa permits you to continue working for your clients or employers abroad while you enjoy everything Colombia has to offer. For many digital nomads, this is a more convenient route than something like an investment visa, as it aligns better with their remote working lifestyle and doesn't necessarily require large amounts of capital.

## 4 benefits of a Colombia digital nomad visa

### 1. Extended stay

With a Colombia digital nomad visa, foreigners can stay in Colombia for a longer duration than typically allowed by a tourist visa. This means you can settle into a favorite neighborhood in Medellín or Bogotá — perhaps El Poblado, a popular choice for young expats in Colombia — where you can build connections and fully experience the daily life that makes this country so appealing to international expats.

### 2. Work legally

Unlike a tourist visa, a digital nomad visa in Colombia offers the legal framework to carry out remote work for [foreign clients or companies](https://www.rippling.com/blog/work-remotely-for-a-us-company). This is a significant advantage over the typical restrictions you might face if you simply visited Colombia on a tourist visa, which wouldn't allow you to engage in work of any kind.

### 3. Cost-effective living

Many international digital nomads find Colombia to be an affordable destination. Daily expenses, from rent to dining, can be significantly lower than in other countries, making it easier to thrive on modest incomes. Whether you prefer the energetic vibe of Bogotá or the laid-back lifestyle of Caribbean coastal towns, you'll likely find a range of budget-friendly options.

### 4. Networking opportunities

The influx of foreign remote workers and freelancers to Colombia has resulted in a rapidly expanding tech and coworking scene. Whether in Medellín or Bogotá, you'll discover numerous coworking spaces, regular meetups, and conferences that are perfect for forging new professional connections. It's easy to meet like-minded digital nomads, entrepreneurs, and expats who can help you explore innovative ideas or collaborate on new projects.

## Advantages of living in Colombia as a digital nomad

There are many reasons why digital nomads are choosing Colombia as a work destination. Here are a few of the most common ones:

*   **Affordable cost of living:**From groceries to rent, many major cities in Colombia can be easier on your wallet than comparable destinations in other countries.

*   **Warm climate and natural beauty:**Whether you love the spring-like weather of Medellín, the cosmopolitan charm of Bogotá, or the coastal allure of Cartagena, there's a climate and scenic backdrop for just about everyone.

*   **Accessible travel options:**Traveling to Colombia has become simpler thanks to multiple international flights and well-connected domestic airlines. It's also a great jumping-off point for visiting neighboring countries in Latin America.

*   **Fast-growing digital nomad community:**The trend of the Medellín digital nomad is real — the expat community in Colombia is thriving. You'll encounter coworking hubs and cafés bustling with remote workers from all over the world.

## Colombia digital nomad visa eligibility

To qualify for a Colombia digital nomad visa, the applicant must have a valid passport from a country exempt from needing a short-stay visa in Colombia. Those countries include (but are not limited to):

*   United States

*   Germany

*   Australia

*   Canada

*   Spain

*   Indonesia

*   Portugal

Applicants also typically need to fit into one of the following categories:

*   [Remote workers or freelancers](https://www.rippling.com/blog/telework-vs-remote-work) working with foreign companies or clients.

*   Entrepreneurs with digital-focused businesses who want to operate in Colombia but do not plan to engage in local employment.

In many cases, immigration authorities will want to confirm that your source of income comes from abroad rather than from a Colombian employer.

## Colombia digital nomad visa requirements

If you're gearing up for a Colombia digital nomad visa, here are some main requirements to keep in mind:

*   **Proof of remote work or freelancing for at least six months:**This may include client contracts, reference letters, or an official letter in Spanish or English describing your remote work arrangement. If you're an entrepreneur, you can submit a motivational letter explaining your work and how it will support your lifestyle in Colombia.

*   **A valid passport:**Make sure your passport is current for the duration of your planned stay, with at least six months of remaining validity.

*   **Passport-style photo** with a white background, taken within the last six months.

*   **Minimum income:**Applicants must show monthly income of at least three times Colombia's minimum monthly wage (SMMLV). As of 2026, that threshold is roughly $1,100–$1,400 USD per month, depending on the exchange rate the Colombian Ministry of Foreign Affairs applies when reviewing your file. Each of the last several months must individually meet the threshold — averaging your income across months isn't accepted, so build in a buffer above the minimum.

*   **Health insurance covering Colombia:**Your policy must explicitly include medical repatriation coverage for the full duration of your stay. General travel insurance typically doesn't qualify; it needs to be a health insurance policy.

*   **Proof of your relationship to any dependents**, if applicable.

Visa requirements can change, so always double-check the latest details from the Colombian consulate or the Cancillería's official immigration website to make sure you have the most up-to-date information.

## Colombia digital nomad visa application

Below is a step-by-step look at how to begin your visa application for the Colombia digital nomad visa. Generally, you'll have to submit all required documents through an online portal or at a Colombian consulate abroad.

### Step 1: Check eligibility

Before you invest time in collecting documents, verify that you meet the basic criteria: Are you a digital nomad working with foreign clients or companies? Can you demonstrate the required income?

### Step 2: Prepare the required documents

Compile your passport, bank statements (the only accepted proof of income — invoices and tax returns alone typically aren't sufficient), insurance policy details with explicit repatriation coverage, and proof of remote work. You might need a formal letter in Spanish explaining your remote work arrangement and how you meet the minimum income threshold.

### Step 3: Submit your application

Start your [online visa application](https://tramitesmre.cancilleria.gov.co/tramites/enlinea/solicitarVisa.xhtml), which can be found on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' online portal. Alternatively, you can visit your nearest Colombian consulate to apply. Be meticulous about uploading the correct documents — missing even a single required file can delay the process.

### Step 4: Pay the application fee

A visa study fee is required to move your application forward, generally around $54 USD. The exact amount can vary depending on the exchange rate between Colombian pesos and USD at the time you apply. Keep in mind there may be additional charges if you're submitting from a consulate abroad.

### Step 5: Wait for approval

Processing times typically run up to 30 calendar days, though they can vary based on application volume and how complete your documentation is. The immigration authorities will review your visa application and notify you of any additional documents needed.

### Step 6: Receive your visa and pay visa fees

Once approved, you'll need to pay an issuance fee before receiving your visa, generally in the $170–$230 USD range depending on exchange rates at the time. Once you've paid, you'll get your Colombia digital nomad visa electronically or via a stamp in your passport. If your visa is valid for more than three months, you'll also need to register with Migración Colombia and obtain a Cédula de Extranjería within 15 days of arrival. From there, you're permitted to live and work remotely in Colombia under the specific terms outlined by the visa.

## Colombia digital nomad visa restrictions

While Colombia's digital nomad visa offers [flexibility to remote workers](https://www.rippling.com/blog/remote-work-software), there are some key restrictions:

### Employment restrictions

You cannot take up local employment with a Colombian company or provide services to Colombian clients, as the digital nomad visa is designed strictly for foreign remote workers who provide services to clients abroad.

### Length of stay

The digital nomad visa allows stays of up to two years, at the discretion of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Time on this visa does not count toward permanent residency. Keep in mind, too, that exceeding the allowed time may lead to penalties or future immigration complications.

### Income requirements

You'll have to maintain the minimum income threshold (three times the SMMLV, roughly $1,100–$1,400 USD/month as of 2026) throughout your stay, with each month individually meeting the bar. Falling below the threshold in any given month could jeopardize your visa status.

### Travel restrictions

While traveling to Colombia is relatively simple, your visa is generally cancelled if you're absent from the country for more than six consecutive months. Check the latest official guidelines to confirm current rules around exits and re-entries on a digital nomad visa.

### Compliance and obligations

Maintaining valid health insurance with repatriation coverage, continuing to meet the income requirements every month, and avoiding unauthorized activities (like taking on local jobs or clients) are part of your obligations as a digital nomad under this visa. Once you cross 183 days in Colombia within any rolling 12-month period, you also become a Colombian tax resident, which means declaring worldwide income — so plan ahead with a tax professional if that threshold applies to you.

## Colombia digital nomad visa vs. tourist visa

While both a tourist visa and a digital nomad visa allow foreigners to stay in Colombia, each serves a distinct purpose and there are key differences between them:

*   **Duration of stay:**A tourist visa generally offers a shorter duration — generally up to 180 days — while the digital nomad visa can allow you to stay for up to two years.

*   **Activities permitted:**On a tourist visa, you're typically not legally allowed to work remotely for extended periods. The digital nomad visa, on the other hand, explicitly permits you to engage in remote work for foreign entities.

*   **Income verification:**A tourist visa does not require you to prove a monthly income, whereas the digital nomad visa does, and requires it every month without averaging.

## Colombia digital nomad visa FAQs

Do digital nomads pay tax in Colombia?

Tax rules can be complex. Digital nomads who spend more than half of the tax year in Colombia may be considered tax residents, depending on specific income and immigration factors. Consult a local tax professional to make sure you’re fully compliant.

How long does it take to get a digital nomad visa in Colombia?

Processing times vary, but most applicants can expect a timeframe of one to three weeks once they’ve submitted all proper documents and paid the necessary application fee and visa fee.

What is the easiest country to get a digital nomad visa?

It can differ based on your personal situation and income level. Besides Colombia, many other countries in Latin America, Europe, and Asia also provide digital nomad visas—and these types of visas are becoming more and more common as countries strive to attract remote workers who can stimulate their economies without taking away local jobs. There are pros and cons in each country, however, and your preference might depend on factors like cost of living, community, climate, and how smoothly the local authorities handle visa applications.

How much income do I need to qualify for Colombia's digital nomad visa?

You need to show monthly income equal to at least three times Colombia's minimum monthly wage (SMMLV). As of 2026, that works out to roughly $1,100–$1,400 USD per month, depending on the exchange rate used when your application is reviewed. Each of your last several months of income statements must individually meet the threshold; averaging is not accepted, so it's wise to apply with a buffer above the minimum.

Can I bring my family on a Colombia digital nomad visa?

Yes. Dependents — such as a spouse or children — can typically be included on your application if you provide proof of the relationship, like a marriage or birth certificate. Each dependent generally needs their own supporting documentation, and consulates may ask for additional proof that you can financially support them during your stay.

Can I work for a Colombian company while on a digital nomad visa?

No. The digital nomad visa is strictly for remote work performed for foreign companies or clients — it doesn't permit local employment or providing services to Colombian clients. If you want to take a job with a Colombian employer, you'll need to apply for a different visa category, such as a work visa sponsored by that employer.

Do I need health insurance for the Colombia digital nomad visa?

Yes, but it must be health insurance with explicit medical repatriation coverage for the full duration of your stay — general travel insurance plans typically don't qualify. Many digital nomads use international or expat-focused health insurance providers that are designed to meet this requirement.

Can I renew my Colombia digital nomad visa?

Colombia's digital nomad visa is valid for up to two years, and renewal is possible, though time on this visa does not count toward permanent residency. To renew, you'll generally need to reapply with updated proof of income, health insurance, and remote work status, following the same process as your original application.

**Costa Rica**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-11) officially the **Republic of Costa Rica**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-12) is a country in [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America"). It borders [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua") to the north, the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea") to the northeast, [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama") to the southeast, and the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") to the southwest, sharing a [maritime border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_boundary "Maritime boundary") with [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador "Ecuador") to the south of [Cocos Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocos_Island "Cocos Island"). It has a population of around five million[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-UN_WPP-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-UN_WPP_2022-14) in a land area of nearly 51,180 km 2 (19,760 sq mi);[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-ignlandarea-15) the capital and largest city is [San José](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jos%C3%A9,_Costa_Rica "San José, Costa Rica"), home to around 350,000 residents and two million people in the surrounding metropolitan area.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-worldscapitalcities.com-16)

Humans have [been in Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_history_of_Costa_Rica "Pre-Columbian history of Costa Rica") since between 7,000 and 10,000 BC. [Various indigenous peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_Costa_Rica "Indigenous peoples of Costa Rica") lived in the territory before it was [colonized by Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") in the 16th century. Costa Rica was a peripheral colony of the Spanish Empire until independence in 1821 as part of the [First Mexican Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Mexican_Empire "First Mexican Empire"), followed by membership in the [Federal Republic of Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Republic_of_Central_America "Federal Republic of Central America") in 1823, from which it formally declared independence in 1847. The country underwent gradual modernization under relatively stable authoritarian rule until the late 19th century, when it promulgated a liberal constitution and held the first free and fair national election in Central America.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-17)

Following [a brief civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_Civil_War "Costa Rican Civil War") in 1948, Costa Rica adopted its [current constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Costa_Rica "Constitution of Costa Rica") in 1949, which granted [universal suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage "Women's suffrage"), provided various social, economic, and educational guarantees for all citizens, and permanently [abolished the army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Force_of_Costa_Rica "Public Force of Costa Rica"), becoming one of the few sovereign [nations without a standing military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_sovereign_states_without_armed_forces "List of sovereign states without armed forces").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-18)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-19)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-20) Costa Rica is a [presidential republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_system "Presidential system") with a robust and stable democracy.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-seattletimes.com-21) About one-fourth of the national budget is spent on education—which has been free and compulsory since 1886—equal to about 6.2% of the country's GDP, compared to a global average of 3.8%;[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-22)[the economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_economy "Costa Rican economy"), once heavily dependent on agriculture, has diversified to include finance, corporate services for foreign companies, pharmaceuticals, and [ecotourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecotourism "Ecotourism").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-cinde.org-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-24)

Costa Rica has consistently performed favorably in the [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Development_Index "Human Development Index") (HDI), placing 62nd globally, and fifth in Latin America, in 2023. Costa Rica is classified by the World Bank as a [high-income economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-income_economy "High-income economy")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-25) and is the only [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD") country in [Central America and the Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-26) It has been cited by the [United Nations Development Programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Development_Programme "United Nations Development Programme") (UNDP) as having attained much higher [human development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_development_(economics) "Human development (economics)") than other countries at the same income levels, with a better record on human development and inequality than the regional median.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-HDI10-27) Costa Rica performs well in metrics of [democratic governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_Index "Democracy Index"), [press freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Press_Freedom_Index "World Press Freedom Index"), [subjective happiness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Happiness_Report "World Happiness Report") and [sustainable wellbeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Planet_Index "Happy Planet Index");[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-28) it has one of the highest literacy rates in the Americas,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-britannica-29) and is considered a regional leader in human rights and environmentalism.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-britannica-29)

## History

Main article: [History of Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Costa_Rica "History of Costa Rica")

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Stone_spheres_of_Costa_Rica._Museo_Nacional.jpg/250px-Stone_spheres_of_Costa_Rica._Museo_Nacional.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stone_spheres_of_Costa_Rica._Museo_Nacional.jpg)

[Stone spheres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_spheres_of_Costa_Rica "Stone spheres of Costa Rica") created by the [Diquis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diquis "Diquis") culture at the [National Museum of Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museo_Nacional_de_Costa_Rica "Museo Nacional de Costa Rica"). [The sphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_spheres_of_Costa_Rica "Stone spheres of Costa Rica") is the icon of the country's cultural identity.

### Pre-Columbian period

Main article: [Pre-Columbian history of Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_history_of_Costa_Rica "Pre-Columbian history of Costa Rica")

Historians have classified the [Indigenous people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") of Costa Rica as belonging to the [Intermediate Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate_Area "Intermediate Area"), where the peripheries of the [Mesoamerican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican "Mesoamerican") and [Andean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andean_world "Andean world") native cultures overlapped. More recently, [pre-Columbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era") Costa Rica has also been described as part of the [Isthmo-Colombian Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isthmo-Colombian_Area "Isthmo-Colombian Area").

Stone tools, the oldest evidence of human occupation in Costa Rica, are associated with the arrival of various groups of [hunter-gatherers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter-gatherer "Hunter-gatherer") about 10,000 to 7,000 years [BCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_Common_Era "Before Common Era") in the [Turrialba Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turrialba_(district) "Turrialba (district)"). The presence of [Clovis culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_culture "Clovis culture") type spearheads and arrows from [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America") opens the possibility that, in this area, two different cultures coexisted.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-precolumbian1-30)

Agriculture became evident in the populations that lived in Costa Rica about 5,000 years ago. They mainly grew [tubers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubers "Tubers") and roots. For the first and second millennia BCE there were already settled farming communities. These were small and scattered, although the timing of the transition from [hunting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter-gatherer "Hunter-gatherer") and gathering to agriculture as the main livelihood in the territory is still unknown.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-precolumbian2-31)

The earliest use of [pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pottery "Pottery") appears around 2,000 to 3,000 BCE. Shards of pots, cylindrical vases, platters, gourds, and other vases decorated with grooves, prints, and some modeled after animals have been found.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-precolumban3-32)

The influence of Indigenous peoples on modern Costa Rican culture has been relatively small compared to other nations since the country lacked a strong native civilization to begin with.[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_][_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Most of the native population was absorbed into the Spanish-speaking [colonial society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas "Spanish colonization of the Americas") through inter-marriage,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] except for some small remnants, the most significant of which are the [Bribri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bribri_people "Bribri people") and [Boruca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boruca_people "Boruca people") tribes who still inhabit the mountains of the [Cordillera de Talamanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cordillera_de_Talamanca "Cordillera de Talamanca"), in the southeastern part of Costa Rica, near the frontier with [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama").

### Spanish colonization

The name _la costa rica_, meaning "rich coast" in the Spanish language, was in some accounts first applied by [Christopher Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus "Christopher Columbus"), who sailed to the eastern shores of Costa Rica during his final voyage in 1502,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-embassy-33) and reported vast quantities of gold jewelry worn by natives.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-lp-34) The name may also have come from conquistador [Gil González Dávila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Gonz%C3%A1lez_D%C3%A1vila "Gil González Dávila"), who landed on the west coast in 1522, encountered natives, and obtained some of their gold, sometimes by violent theft and sometimes as gifts from local leaders.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-35)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bd/Iglesia_Inmaculada_Concepcion_Ujarras.jpg/250px-Iglesia_Inmaculada_Concepcion_Ujarras.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Iglesia_Inmaculada_Concepcion_Ujarras.jpg)

The [Ujarrás](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ujarr%C3%A1s "Ujarrás") historical site in the Orosí Valley, [Cartago province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartago_province "Cartago province"). The church was built between 1686 and 1693.

During most of the colonial period, Costa Rica was the southernmost province of the [Captaincy General of Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captaincy_General_of_Guatemala "Captaincy General of Guatemala"), nominally part of the [Viceroyalty of New Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Spain "New Spain"). The captaincy general was a largely autonomous entity within the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"). Costa Rica's distance from the capital of the captaincy in [Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala "Guatemala"), its legal prohibition under [mercantilist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercantilism "Mercantilism") Spanish law from trade with its southern neighbor Panama, then part of the [Viceroyalty of New Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroyalty_of_New_Granada "Viceroyalty of New Granada") (i.e. [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia")), and lack of resources such as gold and silver, made Costa Rica into a poor, isolated, and sparsely inhabited region within the Spanish Empire.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-36) Costa Rica was described as "the poorest and most miserable Spanish colony in all America" by a Spanish governor in 1719.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-37)

### Independence

See also: [Free State of Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_State_of_Costa_Rica "Free State of Costa Rica") and [First Costa Rican Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Costa_Rican_Republic "First Costa Rican Republic")

Like the rest of [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America"), Costa Rica never fought for independence from Spain. On 15 September 1821, after the final Spanish defeat in the [Mexican War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican_War_of_Independence "Mexican War of Independence") (1810–1821), the authorities in Guatemala declared the independence of all of Central America. That date is still celebrated as Independence Day in Costa Rica[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-38) even though, technically, under the [Spanish Constitution of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Constitution_of_1812 "Spanish Constitution of 1812") that had been readopted in 1820, [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua") and Costa Rica had become an autonomous province with its capital in [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-P%C3%A9rezBrignoli2006-39)

On 3 March 1824, the government of the State of Costa Rica officially proposed to the municipality of [Nicoya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicoya "Nicoya") its voluntary incorporation into the country, through a document in which it invited it "if it was convenient to join its Province without going against its will." On 4 July, an open town hall was convened in Nicoya to discuss the matter, but attendees declined the invitation under the argument "that this Party... cannot be dissident."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-nacion-40)

On 25 July 1824, a second [plebiscite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plebiscite "Plebiscite") was called in the city of Nicoya. After deliberation, the incorporation into Costa Rica was decided in an open town hall meeting, preparing a record in which the main reasons for it were noted, pointing out the advantages in terms of trade, the desire to participate in the advances that are palpable in Costa Rica, the economic, administrative and public service benefits, the creation of schools, security and quiet, referring to the state of war that Nicaragua was experiencing at that time and the fear that it would spread to the Partido populations, in addition to point out the poverty in which its towns find themselves and the geography of the territory as justifications for the union. Three days later, another similar plebiscite was held in [Santa Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Cruz_(canton),_Costa_Rica "Santa Cruz (canton), Costa Rica"), with the same result. The election was by majority vote, with 77% of the Party's population in favor of incorporation, and 23% against it. The town of Guanacaste was the only one that declined annexation, due to the ties its residents had with the city of [Rivas, Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivas,_Nicaragua "Rivas, Nicaragua").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-ActaNicoya1824-41)

Upon independence, Costa Rican authorities faced the issue of officially deciding the future of the country. Two bands formed: the Imperialists, defended by [Cartago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartago,_Costa_Rica "Cartago, Costa Rica") and [Heredia cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heredia_Province "Heredia Province"), which were in favor of [joining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America_under_Mexican_rule "Central America under Mexican rule") the [Mexican Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Mexican_Empire "First Mexican Empire"), and the Republicans, represented by the cities of [San José](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jos%C3%A9,_Costa_Rica "San José, Costa Rica") and [Alajuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alajuela "Alajuela") who defended full independence. Because of the lack of agreement on these two possible outcomes, the first civil war in Costa Rica occurred. The [Battle of Ochomogo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ochomogo "Battle of Ochomogo") took place on the Hill of [Ochomogo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ochomogo "Ochomogo"), located in the [Central Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_Central_Valley "Costa Rican Central Valley") in 1823. The conflict was won by the Republicans and, as a consequence, the city of Cartago lost its status as the capital, which moved to San José.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-42)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-43)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-44)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/First_postal_stamp_CR_4_Reales_1863.jpg/250px-First_postal_stamp_CR_4_Reales_1863.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_postal_stamp_CR_4_Reales_1863.jpg)

1849 [national coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_Costa_Rica "Coat of arms of Costa Rica") was featured in the first postal stamp issued in 1862.

In 1838, long after the [Federal Republic of Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Republic_of_Central_America "Federal Republic of Central America") ceased to function in practice, Costa Rica formally withdrew and proclaimed itself sovereign. The considerable distance and poor communication routes between [Guatemala City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala_City "Guatemala City") and the Central Plateau, where most of the Costa Rican population lived then and still lives now, meant the local population had little allegiance to the federal government in Guatemala. Since colonial times, Costa Rica has been reluctant to become economically tied with the rest of Central America. Even today, despite most of its neighbors'[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-45) efforts to increase regional integration,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-46) Costa Rica has remained more independent.

Until 1849, when it became part of [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama"), [Chiriquí](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiriqu%C3%AD_province "Chiriquí province") was part of Costa Rica. Costa Rican pride was assuaged for the loss of this eastern (or southern) territory with the acquisition of [Guanacaste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanacaste_Province "Guanacaste Province"), in the north.

### Economic growth in the 19th century

See also: [Liberal State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_State "Liberal State")

[Coffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffee "Coffee") was first planted in Costa Rica in 1808,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-47) and by the 1820s, it surpassed [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco"), [sugar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar "Sugar"), and [cacao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cacao_bean "Cacao bean") as a primary [export](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export "Export"). Coffee production remained Costa Rica's principal source of wealth well into the 20th century, creating a wealthy class of growers, the so-called Coffee Barons.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-48) The revenue helped to modernize the country.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-49)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-cafeimports.com-50)

Most of the coffee exported was grown around the main centers of population in the Central Plateau and then transported by [oxcart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullock_cart "Bullock cart") to the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") port of [Puntarenas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puntarenas "Puntarenas") after the main road was built in 1846.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-cafeimports.com-50) By the mid-1850s the main market for coffee was Britain.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-51) It soon became a high priority to develop an effective transportation route from the Central Plateau to the Atlantic Ocean. For this purpose, in the 1870s, the Costa Rican government contracted with U.S. businessman [Minor C. Keith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_C._Keith "Minor C. Keith") to build a railroad from San José to the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Caribbean_Zone "Western Caribbean Zone") port of [Limón](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lim%C3%B3n "Limón"). Despite enormous difficulties with construction, disease, and financing, the railroad was completed in 1890.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-52)

Most Afro-Costa Ricans descend from [Jamaican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica "Jamaica") immigrants who worked in the construction of that railway and now make up about 3% of Costa Rica's population.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] U.S. convicts, Italians, and Chinese immigrants also participated in the construction project. In exchange for completing the railroad, the Costa Rican government granted Keith large tracts of land and a lease on the train route, which he used to produce [bananas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana "Banana") and export them to the United States. As a result, bananas came to rival coffee as the principal Costa Rican export, while foreign-owned corporations (including the [United Fruit Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Fruit_Company "United Fruit Company") later) began to hold a major role in the national economy and eventually became a symbol of the exploitative export economy.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-53) The major labor dispute between the peasants and the United Fruit Company (The Great Banana Strike) was a major event in the country's history and was an important step that would eventually lead to the formation of effective [trade unions in Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_unions_in_Costa_Rica "Trade unions in Costa Rica"), as the company was required to sign a collective agreement with its workers in 1938.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-54)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-55)

### 20th century

See also: [Reform State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_State "Reform State")

Historically, Costa Rica has generally enjoyed greater peace and more consistent political stability than many of its fellow Latin American nations. During the 20th century, however, Costa Rica experienced two significant periods of violence. In 1917–1919, General [Federico Tinoco Granados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Tinoco_Granados "Federico Tinoco Granados") ruled as a military dictator until he was overthrown and forced into exile. The unpopularity of [Tinoco's regime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictatorship_of_the_Tinoco_Brothers "Dictatorship of the Tinoco Brothers") led, after he was overthrown, to a considerable decline in the size, wealth, and political influence of the Costa Rican military. In 1948, [José Figueres Ferrer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Figueres_Ferrer "José Figueres Ferrer") led an armed uprising in the wake of a disputed presidential election between [Rafael Ángel Calderón Guardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_%C3%81ngel_Calder%C3%B3n_Guardia "Rafael Ángel Calderón Guardia") (who had been president between 1940 and 1944) and [Otilio Ulate Blanco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otilio_Ulate_Blanco "Otilio Ulate Blanco").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-56) With more than 2,000 dead, the resulting 44-day [Costa Rican Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_Civil_War "Costa Rican Civil War") was the bloodiest event in Costa Rica during the 20th century.

The victorious rebels formed a government junta that [abolished the military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_Costa_Rica "Military of Costa Rica") all together and oversaw the drafting of a new constitution by a democratically elected assembly.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-nytimes-military-57) Having enacted these reforms, the junta transferred power to Ulate on 8 November 1949. After the _coup d'état_, Figueres became a national hero, winning the country's first democratic election under the new constitution [in 1953](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_general_election,_1953 "Costa Rican general election, 1953"). Starting in 1958, Costa Rica has held additional presidential elections every four years, the latest [in 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Costa_Rican_general_election "2026 Costa Rican general election"). With uninterrupted democracy dating back to at least 1948, the country is the region's most stable.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-peace-58)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-pacifism-59)

## Geography

Main article: [Geography of Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Costa_Rica "Geography of Costa Rica")

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Koppen-Geiger_Map_CRI_present.svg/330px-Koppen-Geiger_Map_CRI_present.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Koppen-Geiger_Map_CRI_present.svg)

Costa Rica map of Köppen climate classification

Costa Rica borders the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea") to the east, and the Pacific Ocean to the west. Costa Rica also borders [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua "Nicaragua") to the north and [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama") to the south.

The highest point in the country is [Cerro Chirripó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Chirrip%C3%B3 "Cerro Chirripó"), at 3,819 metres (12,530 ft). The highest volcano in the country is the [Irazú Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraz%C3%BA_Volcano "Irazú Volcano") (3,431 m or 11,257 ft) and the largest lake is [Lake Arenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Arenal "Lake Arenal"). There are 14 known volcanoes in Costa Rica, and six of them have been active in the last 75 years.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-60)

### Climate

Costa Rica experiences a [tropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_climate "Tropical climate") year-round. There are two seasons. The dry season is December to April, and the rainy season is May to November. March and April are the hottest months in the country, while December and January are the coldest. However, there are rainy days in the dry season, as well as weeks without rain in the wet season.

Costa Rica is highly vulnerable to extreme weather events, which can be exacerbated by [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"). The majority of Costa Rica's population (78%) and economic activity (80% of [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product")) are concentrated in regions highly vulnerable to various natural hazards, such as floods, landslides, cyclones, storm surges, and rising sea levels.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-61) The country is facing increasing temperatures (especially at higher elevations), rising sea levels on both coasts, and changing rainfall patterns resulting in increased risk of drought along the Pacific slope and flooding in all regions of the country.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-62) Increasing temperatures and extreme heat will have major consequences for human health, agriculture (particularly coffee and banana cultivation), water security, tourism, and the country's distinctive biodiversity and ecosystems.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-63)

### Flora and fauna

Further information: [Wildlife of Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildlife_of_Costa_Rica "Wildlife of Costa Rica") and [Conservation in Costa Rica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_in_Costa_Rica "Conservation in Costa Rica")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Scarlet_Macaw.jpg/250px-Scarlet_Macaw.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scarlet_Macaw.jpg)

The [scarlet macaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarlet_macaw "Scarlet macaw") is native to Costa Rica.

Despite its size, Costa Rica is one of the countries with [the greatest biodiversity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildlife_of_Costa_Rica "Wildlife of Costa Rica") in all of [Latin America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America "Latin America").

One national park, the [Corcovado National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corcovado_National_Park "Corcovado National Park"), is internationally renowned among ecologists for its biodiversity (including [big cats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_cats "Big cats") and [tapirs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapirs "Tapirs")) and is where visitors can expect to see an abundance of wildlife.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-64)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-65) Corcovado is the one park in Costa Rica where [all four Costa Rican monkey species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Costa_Rican_monkey_species "List of Costa Rican monkey species") can be found.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-watching-66) These include the [white-headed capuchin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-headed_capuchin "White-headed capuchin"), the [mantled howler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mantled_howler "Mantled howler"), the endangered [Geoffroy's spider monkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffroy's_spider_monkey "Geoffroy's spider monkey"),[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-watching-66)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-67) and the [Central American squirrel monkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_American_squirrel_monkey "Central American squirrel monkey"), found only on the Pacific coast of Costa Rica and a small part of [Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama "Panama") and considered endangered until 2008 when its status was upgraded to vulnerable. [Deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation"), illegal pet trading, and hunting are the main reasons for its threatened status.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-68)[La Amistad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Amistad_International_Park "La Amistad International Park") and [Chirripó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chirrip%C3%B3_National_Park "Chirripó National Park") present the climate of the [páramo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rican_p%C3%A1ramo "Costa Rican páramo"), at a height of more than 3000 meters above sea level, providing other types of flora and fauna, such as the [white-nosed coati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White-nosed_coati "White-nosed coati"), the [sooty thrush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sooty_thrush "Sooty thrush") and _[Rogiera amoena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogiera\_amoena "Rogiera amoena")_. Costa Rica is the first tropical country to have stopped and reversed deforestation; it has successfully restored its forestry and developed an ecosystem service to teach biologists and ecologists about its environmental protection measures.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-69) The country had a 2018 [Forest Landscape Integrity Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Landscape_Integrity_Index "Forest Landscape Integrity Index") mean score of 4.65/10, ranking it 118th globally out of 172 countries.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Rica#cite_note-FLII-Supplementary-70)
