From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Digital nomad visa](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Digital_nomad_visa&redirect=no "Digital nomad visa"))

Authority to enter, stay in, or exit a polity

"Transit visa" redirects here. For other uses, see [Visa (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_(disambiguation) "Visa (disambiguation)").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Visa_usa.jpg/250px-Visa_usa.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Visa_usa.jpg)

A United States travel visa specimen

A **travel****visa** (from[Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language")_charta visa_'paper that has been seen';[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-1) also known as **visa stamp**) is a conditional authorization granted by a [polity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polity "Polity") to a foreigner that allows them to enter, remain within, or leave its territory. Visas typically include limits on the duration of the foreigner's stay, areas within the country they may enter, the dates they may enter, the number of permitted visits, or if the individual can work in the country in question. Visas are associated with the request for permission to enter a territory and thus are, in most countries, distinct from actual formal permission for an [alien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alien_(law) "Alien (law)") to enter and remain in the country. In each instance, a visa is subject to [border control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_control "Border control") at the time of actual entry and can be revoked at any time. Visa evidence most commonly takes the form of a sticker endorsed in the applicant's [passport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passport "Passport") or other [travel document](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travel_document "Travel document") but may also exist electronically. Some countries no longer issue physical visa evidence, instead recording details only in [border security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_security "Border security") databases.

Some countries require that their citizens, and sometimes foreign travelers, obtain an **exit visa** in order to be allowed to leave the country.

Historically, border security officials were empowered to permit or reject entry of visitors on arrival at the frontiers. If a visitor was permitted entry, the official would issue them a visa, when required, as a [stamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passport_stamp "Passport stamp") in a passport. Today, travellers wishing to enter another country must often apply in advance for what is also called a visa, sometimes in person at a [consular office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consulate "Consulate"), by post, or over the Internet. The modern visa may be a sticker or a stamp in the passport, an electronic record of the authorization, or a separate document which the applicant can print before entering and produce on entry to the visited polity. Some countries do not require visitors to apply for a visa in advance for short visits.

Visa applications in advance of arrival give countries a chance to consider the applicant's circumstances, such as financial security, reason for travel, and details of previous visits to the country. Visitors may also be required to undergo and pass security or health checks upon arrival at the port of entry.

Uniquely, the Norwegian special territory of [Svalbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svalbard "Svalbard") is an [entirely visa-free zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_policy_of_Svalbard "Visa policy of Svalbard") under the terms of the [Svalbard Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svalbard_Treaty "Svalbard Treaty").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-2) Some countries—such as those in the [Schengen Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area "Schengen Area")—have agreements with other countries allowing each other's citizens to travel between them without visas. In 2015, the [World Tourism Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Tourism_Organization "World Tourism Organization") announced that the number of tourists requiring a visa before travelling was at its lowest level ever.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-4)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_visa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The history of passports dates back several centuries, originating from early travel documents used to ensure safe passage across regions. One of the earliest known references to a passport-like document comes from 445 BCE in [Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persia "Persia"), where officials were provided letters by the king for safe travel. Similarly, during the [Han Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), documents were required at checkpoints to verify travelers' identities. In [medieval Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), rulers issued "safe conduct" letters that protected travelers. In 1414, during the reign of [King Henry V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_V_of_England "Henry V of England") of [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England"), passports became more formalized, allowing foreigners and citizens to travel safely within England. The 19th century saw an increase in international travel due to the [Industrial Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Revolution "Industrial Revolution"), which led to the widespread adoption of passports, particularly for managing the movement of migrant workers.

In Western Europe in the late 19th century and early 20th century, [passports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passports "Passports") and visas were not generally necessary for moving from one country to another. The relatively high speed and large movements of people travelling by train would have caused bottlenecks if regular passport controls had been used.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-5)

After [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), passports and visas became essential for international travel.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-6) The [League of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/League_of_Nations "League of Nations") convened conferences in the 1920s to standardise passports, setting the foundation for modern versions. The 1920 Paris Conference recommended the adoption of a uniform "international type" ordinary passport to standardize travel documents across countries.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-LeaguePassports1920-7)[_[AI-retrieved source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:AI-retrieved\_source/doc "Template:AI-retrieved source/doc")_] The [International Civil Aviation Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Civil_Aviation_Organization "International Civil Aviation Organization") (ICAO) took over regulation in 1947, leading to machine-readable passports and, eventually, biometric passports in the late 20th century, offering enhanced security and speed in processing travelers.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-10)

## Issuing authorities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_visa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Issuing authorities")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Voucher_for_Myanmar_visa_Bangkok.jpg/250px-Voucher_for_Myanmar_visa_Bangkok.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Voucher_for_Myanmar_visa_Bangkok.jpg)

Passport receipt for visa application, Embassy of Myanmar, Bangkok

Some visas can be granted on arrival or by prior application at the country's embassy or [consulate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consulate "Consulate"), or through a private visa service specialist who is specialized in the issuance of international travel documents. These agencies are authorized by the foreign authority, embassy, or consulate to represent international travellers who are unable or unwilling to travel to the embassy and apply in person. Private visa and passport services collect an additional fee for verifying customer applications, supporting documents, and submitting them to the appropriate authority. If there is no embassy or consulate in one's home country, then one would have to travel to a third country (or apply by post) and try to get a visa issued there. Alternatively, in such cases visas may be pre-arranged for collection on arrival at the border. The need or absence of need of a visa generally depends on the citizenship of the applicant, the intended duration of the stay, and the activities that the applicant may wish to undertake in the country he or she visits; these may delineate different formal categories of visas, with different issue conditions.

The issuing authority, usually a branch of the country's [interior ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_ministry "Interior ministry") or [foreign ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_ministry "Foreign ministry"), or a subordinated agency ([Population and Immigration Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_and_Immigration_Authority "Population and Immigration Authority") in [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel")), and typically consular affairs officers, may request appropriate documentation from the applicant. This may include proof that the applicant has enough money to be self-supporting (or to establish themselves, if the visa is for a long stay or permanent residence), proof that the person or hotel hosting the applicant in his or her home really exists and has sufficient room for hosting the applicant, proof that the applicant has obtained health and evacuation insurance, etc. Some countries ask for proof of health status, especially for long-term visas; some countries deny such visas to persons with certain illnesses, such as [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS"). The exact conditions depend on the country and category of visa. Notable examples of countries requiring [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV "HIV") tests of long-term residents are Russia[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-11) and Uzbekistan.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-voythree-12) In Uzbekistan, however, the HIV test requirement is sometimes not strictly enforced.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-voythree-12) Other countries require a medical test that includes an HIV test, even for a short-term tourism visa. For example, [Cuban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubans "Cubans") citizens and international exchange students require such a test approved by a medical authority to enter Chilean territory.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The issuing authority may also require applicants to attest that they have no criminal convictions, or that they do not participate in certain activities (like prostitution or drug trafficking). Some countries will deny visas if passports show evidence of citizenship of, or travel to, a country that is considered hostile by that country.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Many countries frequently demand strong evidence of intent to return to the home country, if the visa is for a temporary stay, due to potential unwanted [illegal immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_immigration "Illegal immigration"). Proof of ties to the visa applicant's country of residence is often demanded to demonstrate a sufficient incentive to return. This can include things such as documented evidence of employment, bank statements, property ownership, and family ties.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-13)

## Visa politics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_visa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Visa politics")]

The main reasons states impose visa restrictions on foreign nationals are to curb illegal immigration, security concerns, and reciprocity for visa restrictions imposed on their own nationals. Typically, nations impose visa restrictions on citizens of poorer countries, along with politically unstable and undemocratic ones, as it is considered more likely that people from these countries will seek to illegally immigrate. Visa restrictions may also be imposed when nationals of another country are perceived as likelier to be terrorists or criminals, or by autocratic regimes that perceive foreign influence to be a threat to their rule.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-:0-14) According to Professor [Eric Neumayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Neumayer "Eric Neumayer") of the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics"):

> The poorer, the less democratic, and the more exposed to armed political conflict the target country is, the more likely that visa restrictions are in place against its passport holders. The same is true for countries whose nationals have been major perpetrators of terrorist acts in the past.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-:0-14)

The [public support on immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration#Public_support "Immigration") ranges between fully [open borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_borders "Open borders") and fully [closed borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_border#Examples_of_closed_borders "Open border").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-15) Countries can restrict travel visas to prevent [birth tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_tourism "Birth tourism") and [visa fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_fraud "Visa fraud").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-r963-16)[Work permits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_permit "Work permit") can increase the [unemployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unemployment "Unemployment") rate of citizens.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-a450-18)

Some countries apply the principle of [reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_(international_relations) "Reciprocity (international relations)") in their visa policy. Visa reciprocity is a principle in international relations where two countries agree to give each other's citizens similar treatment when it comes to visa requirements.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-19) For example, visa reciprocity is a central principle of the EU's common visa policy. The EU aims to achieve full visa reciprocity with non-EU countries whose citizens can travel to the EU without a visa.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-20) For example, in 2009 Canada reintroduced visa requirements for Czech nationals, arguing it was necessary due to a surge in asylum applications. It raised concerns within the EU about the implications for the common visa policy, the importance of reciprocity in maintaining good relations and ensuring equal treatment for citizens of member states.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-22)

Some polities which restrict [emigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emigration "Emigration") require individuals to possess an [exit visa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exit_visa "Exit visa") to leave the polity.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-23) These exit visas may be required for citizens, foreigners, or both, depending on the policies of the polity concerned. Unlike ordinary visas, exit visas are often seen[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] as an illegitimate intrusion on individuals' right to [freedom of movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_movement "Freedom of movement").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The imposition of an exit visa requirement may be seen to violate [customary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customary_international_law "Customary international law")[international law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_law "International law"), as the right to leave any country is provided for in the [Universal Declaration of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Declaration_of_Human_Rights "Universal Declaration of Human Rights").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-24)

## Visa policies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_visa&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Visa policies")]

Government authorities usually impose administrative entry restrictions on foreign citizens in three ways – countries whose nationals may enter without a visa, countries whose nationals may obtain a visa on arrival, and countries whose nationals require a visa in advance. Nationals who require a visa in advance are usually advised to obtain them at a diplomatic mission of their destination country. Several countries allow nationals of countries that require a visa to obtain them online.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-25)

### Visa exemption agreements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_visa&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Visa exemption agreements")]

See also: [Migration diplomacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_diplomacy "Migration diplomacy") and [Free migration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_migration "Free migration")

Possession of a valid visa is a condition for entry into most countries. However, bilateral exemption schemes exist that permit [free movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_movement "Free movement") between participating states and addition many states permit visa-free entry – known as a **visa waiver**– for short-term tourist visits.

Some countries have [reciprocal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_(international_relations) "Reciprocity (international relations)") agreements such that a visa is not needed under certain conditions, e.g., when the visit is for [tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourism "Tourism") and for a relatively short period. Such reciprocal agreements may stem from common membership in international organizations or a shared heritage:

*   All citizens of [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU) and [EFTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EFTA "EFTA") member countries can travel to and stay in all other EU and EFTA countries without a visa. See [Four Freedoms (European Union)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Freedoms_(European_Union) "Four Freedoms (European Union)") and [Citizenship of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship_of_the_European_Union "Citizenship of the European Union").
*   British and Irish citizens are entitled the right to travel to and live in each other's countries without visas or restrictions under the [Common Travel Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Travel_Area "Common Travel Area") (CTA). Citizens of territories in the CTA do not need visas to travel to and stay in other countries in the CTA.
*   The United States [Visa Waiver Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_Waiver_Program "Visa Waiver Program") allows citizens of 41 countries to travel to the United States without a visa (although a pre-trip entry permission, [ESTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_System_for_Travel_Authorization "Electronic System for Travel Authorization"), is needed).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-32)
*   Citizens of Canada and the United States do not require a visa to travel between the two countries. Historically, verbal declaration of citizenship, or, if requested by an officer, the presentation of one of over 8,000 different types of documents indicating US or Canadian citizenship was sufficient in order to cross the border.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-33) Since the [Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Hemisphere_Travel_Initiative "Western Hemisphere Travel Initiative") came into effect in 2009, a passport, border crossing card, or [enhanced driver's license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_driver's_license "Enhanced driver's license") is now required in order to enter the US from Canada by land, or a passport by air.
*   Any [Gulf Cooperation Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperation_Council_for_the_Arab_States_of_the_Gulf "Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf") (GCC) citizen can enter and stay as long as required in any other GCC member state.
*   All citizens of members of the [Economic Community of West African States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Community_of_West_African_States "Economic Community of West African States") (ECOWAS), excluding those defined by law as undesirable aliens, may enter and stay without a visa in any member state for a maximum period of 90 days. The only requirement is a valid travel document and international vaccination certificates.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-34)
*   Nationals of the [East African Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Community "East African Community") member states do not need visas for entry into any of the member states.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-37)
*   Some countries in the [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") do not require tourist visas of [citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizenship#Commonwealth "Citizenship") of other Commonwealth countries.
*   Citizens of member states of the [Association of Southeast Asian Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Southeast_Asian_Nations "Association of Southeast Asian Nations") do not require tourist visas to visit another member state, with the exception of [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia "Malaysia") and [Myanmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myanmar "Myanmar"); both countries require citizens of the other country to have an eVisa to visit. Until 2009, Burmese citizens were required to have visas to enter all other ASEAN countries. Following the implementation of visa exemption agreements with the other ASEAN countries, in 2016 Burmese citizens are only required to have visas to enter Malaysia.
*   [Commonwealth of Independent States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Independent_States "Commonwealth of Independent States") (CIS) member states mutually allow their citizens to enter visa-free, at least for short stays. There are exceptions between [Tajikistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tajikistan "Tajikistan") and [Uzbekistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uzbekistan "Uzbekistan"), and between [Armenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenia "Armenia") and [Azerbaijan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan").
*   [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") and [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") allow their citizens to enter, live, and work in each other's countries due to the Indo-Nepal friendship treaty of 1951. Indians do not require a visa or passport to travel to [Bhutan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutan "Bhutan") and are only required to obtain passes at the border checkpoints, whilst Bhutan nationals holding a valid [Bhutanese passport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhutanese_passport "Bhutanese passport") are authorized to enter India without a visa.
*   Citizens of [Mercosur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercosur "Mercosur") full member and associate countries can enter without a visa in any of the member and associate countries, just needing to present the ID card.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-mercosur-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-mercosur1-39)

In some cases visa-free entry may be granted to holders of diplomatic passports even as visas are required by normal passport holders (_see: [Passport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passport "Passport")_).

Other countries may unilaterally grant visa-free entry to nationals of certain countries to facilitate tourism, promote business, or even to cut expenses on maintaining consular posts abroad.

Some of the considerations for a country to grant visa-free entry to another country include (but are not limited to):[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

*   being a low security risk for the country potentially granting visa-free entry
*   diplomatic relationship between two countries
*   conditions in the visitor's home country as compared to the host country
*   having a low risk of overstaying or violating visa terms in the country potentially granting visa-free entry

To have a smaller worldwide diplomatic staff, some countries rely on other country's (or countries') judgments when issuing visas. For example, [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico") allows citizens of all countries to enter without Mexican visas if they possess a valid American visa that has already been used. Costa Rica accepts valid visas of [Schengen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_agreement "Schengen agreement")/EU countries, [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan"), [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"), and the United States (if valid for at least three months on date of arrival). The ultimate example of such reliance is the microstate of [Andorra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andorra "Andorra"), which imposes no visa requirements of its own because it has no international airport and is inaccessible by land without passing through the territory of either [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") or [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain") and is thus "protected" by the Schengen visa system.

Visa-free travel between countries also occurs in all cases where passports (or passport-replacing documents such as laissez-passer) are not needed for such travel.

As of 2019, the _Henley & Partners_ passport index ranks the Japanese, Singaporean, and South Korean passports as the ones with the most visa exemptions by other nations, allowing holders of those passports to visit 189 countries without obtaining a visa in advance of arrival.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-40)

### Common area visas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_visa&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Common area visas")]

Normally, visas are valid for entry only into the country that issued the visa. Countries that are members of [regional organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_organization "Regional organization") or party to regional agreements may, however, issue visas valid for entry into some or all of the member states of the organization or agreement:

*   The **[Schengen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Agreement "Schengen Agreement") Visa** is a visa for the [Schengen Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area "Schengen Area"), which consists of most of the [European Economic Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Economic_Area "European Economic Area"), plus several other adjacent countries. The visa allows visitors to stay in the Schengen Area for up to 90 days within a 180-day period[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]. The visa is valid for tourism, family visits, and business.
*   The **Central American Single Visa (Visa Única Centroamericana)** is a visa for Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua. It was implemented by the [CA-4 agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America-4_Border_Control_Agreement "Central America-4 Border Control Agreement"). It allows citizens of those four countries free access to other member countries. It also allows visitors to any member country to enter another member country without having to obtain another visa.

#### Possible common visa schemes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_visa&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Possible common visa schemes")]

Potentially, there are new common visa schemes:

*   An **[ASEAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASEAN "ASEAN") common visa scheme** has been considered with Thailand and the "CLMV" countries of Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, and Vietnam opting in earlier. After talk arose of a CLMV common visa,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-ttg-41) with Thailand being omitted, Thailand initiated and began implementation of a trial common visa with Cambodia, but cited security risks as the major hurdle. The trial run was delayed,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-42) but Thailand implemented a single visa scheme with Cambodia beginning on 27 December 2012 on a trial basis.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-43)
*   A [Gulf Cooperation Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Cooperation_Council "Gulf Cooperation Council") single visa has been recommended as a study submitted to the council.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-44)
*   The [Pacific Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Alliance "Pacific Alliance"), which currently consists of [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile "Chile"), [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia"), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico "Mexico"), and [Peru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peru "Peru"), offer a common visa for tourism purposes only in order to make it easier for nationals from countries outside of the alliance to travel through these countries by not having to apply for multiple visas.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-45)
*   An **[East African Single Tourist Visa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Community#Single_tourist_visa "East African Community")** is under consideration by the relevant sectoral authorities under the [East African Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Community "East African Community") (EAC) integration program. If approved the visa will be valid for all five partner states in the EAC ([Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"), [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania"), [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda"), [Rwanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda "Rwanda"), and [Burundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burundi "Burundi")). Under the proposal for the visa, any new East African single visa can be issued by any partner state's embassy. The visa proposal followed an appeal by the tourist boards of the partner states for a common visa to accelerate promotion of the region as a single tourist destination and the EAC Secretariat wants it approved before November's World Travel Fair (or [World Travel Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Travel_Market?action=edit&redlink=1 "World Travel Market (page does not exist)")) in London.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-46) When approved by the East African council of ministers, tourists could apply for one country's entry visa, which would then be applicable in all regional member states as a single entry requirement initiative.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-47) This is considered also by [COMESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COMESA "COMESA").
*   The **SADC UNIVISA** (or **Univisa**) has been in development since [Southern African Development Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_African_Development_Community "Southern African Development Community") (SADC) members signed a Protocol on the Development of Tourism in 1998. The Protocol outlined the Univisa as an objective so as to enable the international and regional entry and travel of visitors to occur as smoothly as possible.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] It was expected to become operational by the end of 2002.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-autogenerated4-48) Its introduction was delayed and a new implementation date, the end of 2006, was announced. The univisa was originally intended to only be available, initially, to visitors from selected "source markets" including Australia, the [Benelux countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benelux_countries "Benelux countries"), France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Portugal, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-autogenerated4-48) It is now expected that when the Univisa is implemented, it will apply to non-SADC international (long-haul) tourists travelling to and within the region and that it will encourage multi – destination travel within the region. It is also anticipated that the Univisa will enlarge tourist market for transfrontier parks by lowering the boundaries between neighbouring countries in the parks. The visa is expected to be valid for all the countries with trans frontier parks (Botswana, Lesotho, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, and Zimbabwe) and some other SADC countries (Angola and Swaziland).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-autogenerated3-49) As of 2017, universal visa is implemented by [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") and [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"). Nationals of 65 countries and territories are eligible for visa on arrival that is valid for both countries. This visa is branded _KAZA Uni-visa programme_ after [Kavango–Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kavango%E2%80%93Zambezi_Transfrontier_Conservation_Area "Kavango–Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area") (KAZA). It is expected that other SADC countries will join the program in the future.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_nomad_visa#cite_note-50)

These ten member countries had agreed to form a "Single Domestic Space" in which travellers would only have their passport stamped and have to submit completed, standardized entry and departure forms at the first port and country of entry. The CARICOM Visa was applicable to the nationals of all countries except CARICOM member states (other than Haiti) and associate member states, Canada, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, South Africa, the United Kingdom, the United States of America, and the overseas countries, territories, or departments of these countries. The CARICOM Visa could be obtained from the Embassies/Consulates of Barbados, Jamaica, and Trinidad & Tobago and in countries that have no CARICOM representatives, the applications forms could be obtained from the embassies and consulates of the United Kingdom. The common visa was only intended for the duration of the [2007 Cricket World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Cricket_World_Cup "2007 Cricket World Cup") and was discontinued on 15 May 2007. Discussions are ongoing into instituting a revised CARICOM visa on a permanent basis in the future.
*   A predecessor of the Schengen common visa was the [Benelux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benelux "Benelux") visa. Visas issued by Belgium, Netherlands, and Luxembourg were valid for all the three countries.

### Entry and duration period

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Travel_visa&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Entry and duration period")]

Visas can also be _single-entry_, which means the visa is cancelled as soon as the holder enters the country; _double-entry_; or _multiple-entry_, which permits double or multiple entries into the country with the same visa. Countries may also issue [re-entry permits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-entry_permit "Re-entry permit") that allow temporarily leaving the country without invalidating the visa. Even a business visa will normally not allow the holder to work in the host country without an additional [work permit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_permit "Work permit").

Once issued, a visa will typically have to be used within a certain period of time.

In some countries, the validity of a visa is not the same as the authorized period of stay. The visa validity then indicates the time period when the entry is permitted into the country. For example, if a visa has been issued to begin on 1 January and to expire on 30 March, and the typical authorized period of stay in a country is 90 days, then the 90-day authorized stay starts on the day the passenger enters the country (entrance has to be between 1 January and 30 March). Thus, the latest day the traveller could conceivably stay in the issuing country is 1 July (if the traveller entered on 30 March). This interpretation of visas is common in the Americas.

With other countries, a person may not stay beyond the period of validity of their visa, which is usually set within the period of validity of their passport. The visa may also limit the total number of days the visitor may spend in the applicable territory within the period of validity. This interpretation of visa periods is common in Europe.

Once in the country, the validity period of a visa or authorized stay can often be extended for a fee at the discretion of immigration authorities. Overstaying a period of authorized stay given by the immigration officers is considered [illegal immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_immigration "Illegal immigration") even if the visa validity period is not over (i.e., for multiple entry visas) and a form of being "out of status" and the offender may be [fined](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_(penalty) "Fine (penalty)"), prosecuted, [deported](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportation "Deportation"), or even [blacklisted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blacklist "Blacklist")

**Nicaragua**,[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-19) officially the **Republic of Nicaragua**,[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-20) is a [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") in [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America"), comprising 130,370 square kilometers (50,340 sq mi). With a population of 7,097,329 as of 2026,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-21) it is the third-most populous country in Central America after [Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala "Guatemala") and [Honduras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras "Honduras"), and the [largest by area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_North_American_countries_by_area "List of North American countries by area") in all of Central America.

Nicaragua is bordered by Honduras to the north, the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea") of the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") to the east, Costa Rica to the south, and the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") to the west. The country also shares maritime borders with [El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador") to the west and [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") to the east. Nicaragua's largest city and national capital is [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua"), which is also the [fourth-largest city in Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_cities_in_Central_America#Largest_cities_proper "List of largest cities in Central America"), with a population of 1,055,247 as of December 2020. Nicaragua is known as "the breadbasket of Central America" due to having the most fertile soil and arable land in all of Central America.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-22)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-23) The official language is [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"), though different groups on the Caribbean coast ([Mosquitia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_Coast "Mosquito Coast")) speak their own languages and [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"). The mixture of cultural traditions has generated substantial diversity in folklore, cuisine, music, and literature, including contributions by Nicaraguan poets and writers such as [Rubén Darío](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rub%C3%A9n_Dar%C3%ADo "Rubén Darío").

Originally inhabited by various indigenous cultures since ancient times, the region was conquered by the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") in the 16th century. Nicaragua gained independence from Spain in 1821. The Caribbean region ([Mosquitia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_Coast "Mosquito Coast")) followed a different historical path, being an independent kingdom under British protection from the 17th century until 1860 with the signing of the [Treaty of Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Managua "Treaty of Managua"), which brought it into a [union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_union "Real union") with Nicaragua, while its northernmost part was placed under Honduras by the Wyke-Cruz Treaty of 1859.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-24) Since its independence, Nicaragua has undergone periods of political unrest, dictatorship, [American occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Nicaragua "United States occupation of Nicaragua") and fiscal crisis, as well as the [Nicaraguan Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaraguan_Revolution "Nicaraguan Revolution") of the 1960s and 1970s and the [Contra War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contras "Contras") of the 1980s.

Though nominally a unitary presidential republic, Nicaragua has experienced significant [democratic backsliding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_backsliding "Democratic backsliding") since 2007 under the presidency of [Daniel Ortega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Ortega "Daniel Ortega"), resulting in [large protests in 2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Nicaraguan_protests "2018 Nicaraguan protests") and a subsequent crackdown. Following the [2021 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Nicaraguan_general_election "2021 Nicaraguan general election"), it has been widely described as an [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism")[dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictatorship "Dictatorship"),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-25)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-26)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-27) and the [next national elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_Nicaraguan_general_election "Next Nicaraguan general election") were effectively canceled in 2026.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-28)[_[not verified in body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] It is a developing country and has the [second lowest GDP per capita (nominal)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_American_and_Caribbean_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of Latin American and Caribbean countries by GDP (nominal)") and [fourth lowest GDP per capita (PPP)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_American_and_Caribbean_countries_by_GDP_(PPP) "List of Latin American and Caribbean countries by GDP (PPP)") among Latin American and Caribbean countries. In 2025, Nicaragua was ranked as the second-most corrupt country in Latin America, after [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela"), by the [Corruption Perceptions Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_Perceptions_Index#2020%E2%80%932024 "Corruption Perceptions Index"). Nicaragua's multiethnic population includes people of [mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"), indigenous, European, and African heritage.

Known as the "land of lakes and volcanoes",[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brierley-29)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Wallace-30) Nicaragua is also home to the [Bosawás Biosphere Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosaw%C3%A1s_Biosphere_Reserve "Bosawás Biosphere Reserve"), the second-largest tropical rainforest of the Americas.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-31) The biological diversity, warm tropical climate and active volcanoes have made Nicaragua an increasingly popular [tourist destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_destination "Tourist destination").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-32)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-33) Nicaragua is a founding member of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations")[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-34) and is also a member of the [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement"),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-35)[Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivarian_Alliance_for_the_Peoples_of_Our_America "Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-36) and [Community of Latin American and Caribbean States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_of_Latin_American_and_Caribbean_States "Community of Latin American and Caribbean States").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-37)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Gran_Nicoya.jpg/250px-Gran_Nicoya.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gran_Nicoya.jpg)

Location of _Nicanahuac_, the Indigenous name for _[Gran Nicoya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran\_Nicoya?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gran Nicoya (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran%20Nicoya "es:Gran Nicoya")]_, an area in western Nicaragua and northwestern Costa Rica inhabited by the Nahuas

The etymology of Nicaragua is _Nicānāhuac_, which was the name the [Nicaraos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicarao_people "Nicarao people"), a [Nawat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawat "Nawat")-speaking people, gave to the [Greater Nicoya](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran%20Nicoya "es:Gran Nicoya") region of Nicaragua and Costa Rica.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-38)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-39)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-cclec.org-40)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-41)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-42)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-43)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-44) It means "here lies Anahuac" in Nahuatl and is a combination of the words "nican" (here),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-45) and "[Ānāhuac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anahuac_(Aztec) "Anahuac (Aztec)")", which is a combination of the words "atl" (water) and "nahuac", a locative meaning "surrounded". Therefore, the literal translation of _Nicanahuac_ is "here surrounded by water", which corraborates the theory that the etymology refers to the large bodies of water in and around the country, the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean"), lakes [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") and [Xolotlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Xolotlan "Lake Xolotlan"), and the rivers and lagoons. The name evolved through phonetic changes such as the "n" becoming an _r_ and the _ahuac_ in "anahuac" becoming _agua_ as both "anahuac" and "agua" relate to the concept of water, which would have made it a convenient circumstance for the Spanish in renaming _Nicanahuac_ to _Nicaragua_.

Previous theories about the country's name came from the following: _nican-nahua_, which means "here are the Nahuas"; and [nicarao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicarao_(cacique) "Nicarao (cacique)")-agua. However, in 2002, it was discovered that the real name of the cacique was Macuilmiquiztli and not Nicarao, ultimately debunking this theory.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-46)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-47)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-48)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-49)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-cclec.org-40)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Ideal-50)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Pueblo-51)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Choque-52)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-53)

### Pre-Columbian history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Pre-Columbian history")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Nicaragua_Ometepe_p%C3%A9troglyphes_1.jpg/250px-Nicaragua_Ometepe_p%C3%A9troglyphes_1.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nicaragua_Ometepe_p%C3%A9troglyphes_1.jpg)

An ancient [petroglyph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroglyph "Petroglyph") on [Ometepe Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ometepe_Island "Ometepe Island")

[Paleo-Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleo-Indians "Paleo-Indians") first inhabited what is now known as Nicaragua as far back as 12,000 BCE.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Dall2005-54) In later [pre-Columbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Columbian_era "Pre-Columbian era") times, Nicaragua's [indigenous people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Indigenous peoples of the Americas") were part of the [Intermediate Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate_Area "Intermediate Area"),[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):33 between the [Mesoamerican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerica "Mesoamerica") and [Andean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes "Andes") cultural regions, and within the influence of the [Isthmo-Colombian Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isthmo-Colombian_Area "Isthmo-Colombian Area"). Nicaragua's central region and its Caribbean coast were inhabited by [Macro-Chibchan language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macro-Chibchan_languages "Macro-Chibchan languages") ethnic groups such as the [Miskito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miskito_people "Miskito people"), [Rama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rama_people "Rama people"), [Mayangna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayagna "Mayagna"), and [Matagalpas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cacaopera_people "Cacaopera people").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):20 They had coalesced in Central America and migrated both to and from present-day northern Colombia and nearby areas.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-56) Their food came primarily from hunting and gathering, but also fishing and [slash-and-burn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slash-and-burn "Slash-and-burn") agriculture.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):33[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-57)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):65

At the end of the 15th century, western Nicaragua was inhabited by several indigenous peoples related by culture to the Mesoamerican civilizations of the [Aztec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztecs "Aztecs") and [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_peoples "Maya peoples"), and by language to the [Mesoamerican language area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_language_area "Mesoamerican language area").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-LOC1-59) The [Mangue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangue_people "Mangue people"), or Chorotega, were an ethnic group who had arrived in Nicaragua from what is now the Mexican state of [Chiapas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiapas "Chiapas") sometime around 800 CE.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Choque-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):26–33 The [Nicarao people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicarao_people "Nicarao people") were a branch of [Nahuas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahuas "Nahuas") who spoke the [Nawat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawat_language "Nawat language") dialect and also came from Chiapas, around 1200 CE.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Campbell1985-60) Prior to that, the Nicaraos had been associated with the [Toltec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toltec "Toltec") civilization.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):26–33[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Campbell1985-60)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-61)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-62)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-63)

Both Chorotegas and Nicaraos originated in Mexico's [Cholula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholula_(Mesoamerican_site) "Cholula (Mesoamerican site)") valley,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Campbell1985-60) and migrated south.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):26–33 A third group, the [Subtiabas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subtiaba_language "Subtiaba language"), were an [Oto-Manguean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oto-Manguean_languages "Oto-Manguean languages") people who migrated from the Mexican state of [Guerrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrero "Guerrero") around 1200 CE.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Campbell1997-64):159 Additionally, there were trade-related colonies in Nicaragua set up by the Aztecs starting in the 14th century.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):26–33
