The colonial city of [Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua "Granada, Nicaragua") near [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua"), one of the most visited sites in [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America")

In 1502, on his fourth voyage, [Christopher Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus "Christopher Columbus") became the first European known to have reached what is now Nicaragua as he sailed southeast toward the [Isthmus of Panama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isthmus_of_Panama "Isthmus of Panama").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):193[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):92 Columbus explored the [Mosquito Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_Coast "Mosquito Coast") on the Atlantic side of Nicaragua[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-65) but did not encounter any indigenous people. 20 years later, the Spaniards returned to Nicaragua, this time to its southwestern part. The first attempt to conquer Nicaragua was by the conquistador [Gil González Dávila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Gonz%C3%A1lez_D%C3%A1vila "Gil González Dávila"),[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-EBH-66) who had arrived in Panama in January 1520.

In 1522, González Dávila ventured to the area that later became the [Rivas Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rivas_Department "Rivas Department") of Nicaragua.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):35[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):92 There he encountered an indigenous Nahua tribe led by chief Macuilmiquiztli, whose name has sometimes been erroneously referred to as "[Nicarao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicarao_(cacique) "Nicarao (cacique)")" or "Nicaragua". The tribe's capital was Quauhcapolca.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Encuentro-67)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-HealyPohl1980-68)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Dyck2015-69) González Dávila conversed with Macuilmiquiztli thanks to two indigenous interpreters who had learned Spanish, whom he had brought along.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Sanchez-70)

After exploring and gathering gold[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Encuentro-67)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):35[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):55 in the fertile western valleys, González Dávila and his men were attacked and driven off by the Chorotega, led by chief [Diriangén](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diriangen "Diriangen").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Encuentro-67)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-71) The Spanish tried to convert the tribes to Christianity; Macuilmiquiztli's tribe was baptized,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Encuentro-67)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):86 but Diriangén was openly hostile to the Spaniards. Western Nicaragua, at the Pacific Coast, became a port and shipbuilding facility for the [Galleons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Galleon "Manila Galleon") plying the waters between [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila") and [Acapulco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acapulco "Acapulco").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-72)

In 1524, the first Spanish permanent settlements were founded.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-EBH-66) That year, the conquistador [Francisco Hernández de Córdoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Hern%C3%A1ndez_de_C%C3%B3rdoba_(founder_of_Nicaragua) "Francisco Hernández de Córdoba (founder of Nicaragua)") founded two of Nicaragua's main cities: [Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada,_Nicaragua "Granada, Nicaragua") on [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua"), and then [León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n,_Nicaragua "León, Nicaragua"), west of [Lake Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Managua "Lake Managua").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):35,193[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):92 Córdoba soon built defenses for the cities and fought against incursions by other conquistadors.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):92 Córdoba was later publicly beheaded for having defied his superior, [Pedro Arias Dávila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Arias_D%C3%A1vila "Pedro Arias Dávila").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):35 Córdoba's tomb and remains were discovered in 2000 in the [ruins of León Viejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n_Viejo "León Viejo").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-ET-73)

The clashes among Spanish forces did not impede their destruction of the indigenous people and their culture. The series of battles came to be known as the "War of the Captains".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-74) Pedro Arias Dávila was a winner;[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):35 although he lost control of Panama, he moved to Nicaragua and established his base in León.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Whisnant2000-75) In 1527, León became the capital of the colony.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):93[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Whisnant2000-75) Through diplomacy, Arias Dávila became the colony's first governor.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-ET-73)

Without women in their parties,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):123 the Spanish conquerors took Nahua and Chorotega wives and partners, beginning the multiethnic mix of indigenous and European stock now known as "_[mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo")_", which constitutes the great majority of the population in western Nicaragua.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-LOC1-59) Many indigenous people were killed by European [infectious diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infectious_disease "Infectious disease"), compounded by neglect by the Spaniards, who controlled their subsistence.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-EBH-66) Many other indigenous peoples were captured and transported as slaves to Panama and Peru between 1526 and 1540.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):193[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Newson-58):104–105

In 1610, the [Momotombo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momotombo "Momotombo") volcano erupted, destroying the city of León.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Geomorph-76) The city was rebuilt northwest of the original,[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Whisnant2000-75)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Geomorph-76) which is now known as the [ruins of León Viejo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le%C3%B3n_Viejo "León Viejo"). During the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), Central America was subject to conflict between Britain and Spain. British navy admiral [Horatio Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Nelson "Horatio Nelson") led expeditions in the [Battle of San Fernando de Omoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_San_Fernando_de_Omoa "Battle of San Fernando de Omoa") in 1779 and on the [San Juan River in 1780](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan_Expedition_(1780) "San Juan Expedition (1780)"), the latter of which had temporary success before being abandoned due to disease.

### Independent Nicaragua (1821–1909)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Independent Nicaragua (1821–1909)")]

See also: [History of Nicaragua §Fight for independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Nicaragua#Fight_for_independence "History of Nicaragua")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Political_Evolution_of_Central_America_and_the_Caribbean_1830_na.png/250px-Political_Evolution_of_Central_America_and_the_Caribbean_1830_na.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Political_Evolution_of_Central_America_and_the_Caribbean_1830_na.png)

The [Mosquito Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_Coast "Mosquito Coast") in 1830

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/La_Pedrada_de_Andres_Castro.jpg/250px-La_Pedrada_de_Andres_Castro.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:La_Pedrada_de_Andres_Castro.jpg)

A portrait of the [Battle of San Jacinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_San_Jacinto_(1856) "Battle of San Jacinto (1856)") during the [Filibuster War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_War "Filibuster War")

The [Act of Independence of Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Independence_of_Central_America "Act of Independence of Central America") dissolved the [Captaincy General of Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captaincy_General_of_Guatemala "Captaincy General of Guatemala") in September 1821, and Nicaragua soon [became part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America_under_Mexican_rule "Central America under Mexican rule") of the [First Mexican Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Mexican_Empire "First Mexican Empire"). In July 1823, after the overthrow of the Mexican monarchy in March of the same year, Nicaragua joined the newly formed [United Provinces of Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Republic_of_Central_America "Federal Republic of Central America"), a country later known as the Federal Republic of Central America. Nicaragua definitively became an independent republic in 1838.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-77)

The early years of independence were characterized by rivalry between the [Liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutionalist_Liberal_Party "Constitutionalist Liberal Party") elite of León and the [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(Nicaragua) "Conservative Party (Nicaragua)") elite of Granada, which often degenerated into civil war, particularly during the 1840s and 1850s. [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") rose to undisputed preeminence as the nation's capital in 1852 to allay the rivalry between the two feuding cities.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Capital-78)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-79) Following the start of the [California Gold Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Gold_Rush "California Gold Rush") in 1848, Nicaragua provided a route for travelers from the eastern United States to journey to [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California") by sea, via the [San Juan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan_River_(Nicaragua) "San Juan River (Nicaragua)") and Lake Nicaragua.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):81

Invited by the Liberals in 1855 to join their struggle against the Conservatives, the American adventurer and [filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filibuster_(military) "Filibuster (military)")[William Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Walker_(filibuster) "William Walker (filibuster)") set himself up as [President of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Nicaragua "President of Nicaragua") after conducting a farcical election in 1856; his presidency lasted less than a year.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-mined-80) Military forces from Costa Rica, Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, and Nicaragua itself united to drive Walker out of Nicaragua in 1857,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-81)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-82)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-83) bringing three decades of Conservative rule.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-84)

Great Britain, which had a formal [protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protectorate "Protectorate") over the [Kingdom of Mosquitia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_Coast "Mosquito Coast") since 1655, delegated its northern area to Honduras in 1859, and its middle region to Nicaragua in 1860. Mosquitia remained semi-independent until the [Nicaragua Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_Crisis_of_1894%E2%80%931895 "Nicaragua Crisis of 1894–1895") in 1894, when it was militarily occupied by orders of [José Santos Zelaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Santos_Zelaya "José Santos Zelaya"), President of Nicaragua, who later renamed the territory "[Zelaya Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zelaya_Department "Zelaya Department")".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-85)

Throughout the late 19th century, the United States and several European powers considered various schemes to link the Pacific Ocean to the Atlantic by building a [canal across Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_Canal "Nicaragua Canal").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-86)

### United States occupation (1909–1933)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: United States occupation (1909–1933)")]

See also: [United States occupation of Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Nicaragua "United States occupation of Nicaragua")

In 1909, the United States supported the forces rebelling against President Zelaya. U.S. motives included differences over the proposed [Nicaragua Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_Canal "Nicaragua Canal"), Nicaragua's potential to destabilize the region, and Zelaya's attempts to regulate foreign access to Nicaraguan natural resources. On 18 November 1909, U.S. warships were sent to the area after 500 revolutionaries (including two Americans) were executed by order of Zelaya. The U.S. justified the intervention by claiming to protect U.S. lives and property. Zelaya resigned later that year.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In August 1912, the President of Nicaragua, [Adolfo Díaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolfo_D%C3%ADaz "Adolfo Díaz"), requested the secretary of war, General [Luis Mena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Mena_(Nicaraguan_politician) "Luis Mena (Nicaraguan politician)"), to resign for fear he was leading an insurrection. Mena fled Managua with his brother, the chief of police of Managua, to start an insurrection. After Mena's troops captured steam boats of an American company, the U.S. delegation asked President Díaz to ensure the safety of American citizens and property during the insurrection. He replied he could not, and asked the U.S. to intervene in the conflict.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-87)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-88)

[U.S. Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps") occupied Nicaragua from 1912 to 1933,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brief-55):111,197 except for a nine-month period beginning in 1925. In 1914, the [Bryan–Chamorro Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bryan%E2%80%93Chamorro_Treaty "Bryan–Chamorro Treaty") was signed, giving the U.S. control over a proposed canal through Nicaragua, as well as leases for potential canal defenses.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-89) After the U.S. Marines left, another [violent conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaraguan_civil_war_(1926%E2%80%9327) "Nicaraguan civil war (1926–27)") between Liberals and Conservatives in 1926 resulted in the return of U.S. Marines.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-90)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8a/General_Sandino_%28center%29_and_Staff_enroute_to_Mexico._Siglo_XX.%2C_06-1929_-_NARA_-_532357.tif/lossy-page1-250px-General_Sandino_%28center%29_and_Staff_enroute_to_Mexico._Siglo_XX.%2C_06-1929_-_NARA_-_532357.tif.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:General_Sandino_(center)_and_Staff_enroute_to_Mexico._Siglo_XX.,_06-1929_-_NARA_-_532357.tif)

Rebel leader [Augusto César Sandino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_C%C3%A9sar_Sandino "Augusto César Sandino") (center) in June 1929

From 1927 to 1933, rebel general [Augusto César Sandino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augusto_C%C3%A9sar_Sandino "Augusto César Sandino") led a sustained guerrilla war against the regime and then against the [U.S. Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marines "United States Marines"), whom he fought for over five years.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-91) When the Americans left in 1933, they set up the _[Guardia Nacional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Guard\_(Nicaragua) "National Guard (Nicaragua)")_ (national guard),[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-SY-92) a combined military and police force trained and equipped by the Americans and designed to be loyal to U.S. interests.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

After the U.S. Marines withdrew from Nicaragua in January 1933, Sandino and the newly elected administration of President [Juan Bautista Sacasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Bautista_Sacasa "Juan Bautista Sacasa") reached an agreement that Sandino would cease his guerrilla activities in return for amnesty, a land grant for an agricultural colony, and retention of an armed band of 100 men for a year.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-93) However, due to a growing hostility between Sandino and National Guard director [Anastasio Somoza García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastasio_Somoza_Garc%C3%ADa "Anastasio Somoza García") and a fear of armed opposition from Sandino, Somoza García ordered his assassination.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-SY-92)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-94)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-95)

Sacasa invited Sandino for dinner and to sign a peace treaty at the Presidential House on the night of 21 February 1934. After leaving the Presidential House, Sandino's car was stopped by National Guard soldiers and they kidnapped him. Later that night, Sandino was assassinated by National Guard soldiers. Later, hundreds of men, women, and children from Sandino's agricultural colony were murdered.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-SomozaDynasty-96)

### Somoza dynasty (1936–1979)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Somoza dynasty (1936–1979)")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Trujillo-Somoza_1952.jpg/250px-Trujillo-Somoza_1952.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trujillo-Somoza_1952.jpg)

President [Anastasio Somoza García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastasio_Somoza_Garc%C3%ADa "Anastasio Somoza García") (left) with [Dominican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Republic "Dominican Republic") President [Rafael Trujillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Trujillo "Rafael Trujillo") in 1952

Nicaragua has experienced several military dictatorships, the longest being the hereditary dictatorship of the [Somoza family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somoza_family "Somoza family"), who ruled for 43 nonconsecutive years during the 20th century.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-97) The Somoza family came to power in 1937 partly as a result of a U.S.-engineered pact in 1927 that stipulated the formation of the _Guardia Nacional_ to replace the marines who had long reigned in the country.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-98) Somoza García slowly eliminated officers in the national guard who might have stood in his way, and then deposed Sacasa and became president on 1 January 1937, in a [rigged election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-SY-92)

In 1941, during the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), Nicaragua declared war on [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan "Empire of Japan") (8 December), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") (11 December), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy") (11 December), [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bulgaria "Kingdom of Bulgaria") (19 December), [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary_(1920%E2%80%931946) "Kingdom of Hungary (1920–1946)") (19 December) and [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Romania "Kingdom of Romania") (19 December). Only Romania reciprocated, declaring war on Nicaragua on the same day (19 December 1941).[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-99) No soldiers were sent to the war, but Somoza García confiscated properties held by [German Nicaraguan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Nicaraguan "German Nicaraguan") residents.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-100) In 1945, Nicaragua was among the first countries to ratify the United Nations Charter.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-101)

On 29 September 1956,[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-102) Somoza García was shot to death by [Rigoberto López Pérez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigoberto_L%C3%B3pez_P%C3%A9rez "Rigoberto López Pérez"), a 27-year-old Liberal Nicaraguan poet. [Luis Somoza Debayle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Somoza_Debayle "Luis Somoza Debayle"), the eldest son of the late president, was appointed president by the congress and officially took charge of the country.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-SY-92) He is remembered by some as moderate, but after only a few years in power died of a heart attack. His successor as president was [René Schick Gutiérrez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Schick_Guti%C3%A9rrez "René Schick Gutiérrez"), whom most Nicaraguans viewed "as nothing more than a puppet of the Somozas".[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-103) Somoza García's youngest son, [Anastasio Somoza Debayle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anastasio_Somoza_Debayle "Anastasio Somoza Debayle"), often referred to simply as "Somoza", became president in 1967.

An [earthquake in 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Nicaragua_earthquake "1972 Nicaragua earthquake") destroyed nearly 90% of Managua, including much of its infrastructure.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-104) Instead of helping to rebuild the city, Somoza Debayle siphoned off relief money. The mishandling of relief money also prompted [Pittsburgh Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Pirates "Pittsburgh Pirates") star [Roberto Clemente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Clemente "Roberto Clemente") to personally fly to Managua on 31 December 1972, but he died _en route_ in an airplane accident.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-105)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-106) Even the economic elite were reluctant to support Somoza, as he had acquired monopolies in industries that were key to rebuilding the nation.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-107)

The Somoza family was among a few families or groups of influential firms which reaped most of the benefits of the country's growth from the 1950s to the 1970s. When Somoza was deposed by the Sandinistas in 1979, the family's worth was estimated to be between $500 million and $1.5 billion.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-108)

### Nicaraguan Revolution (1961–1990)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Nicaraguan Revolution (1961–1990)")]

Main articles: [Nicaraguan Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaraguan_Revolution "Nicaraguan Revolution") and [History of Nicaragua (1979–1990)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Nicaragua_(1979%E2%80%931990) "History of Nicaragua (1979–1990)")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/10th_anniversary_of_the_Nicaraguan_revolution_in_Managua%2C_1989.jpg/250px-10th_anniversary_of_the_Nicaraguan_revolution_in_Managua%2C_1989.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:10th_anniversary_of_the_Nicaraguan_revolution_in_Managua,_1989.jpg)

Celebrations of the 10th anniversary of the [Nicaraguan Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaraguan_Revolution "Nicaraguan Revolution") in [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua") in 1989

In 1961, [Carlos Fonseca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Fonseca "Carlos Fonseca") looked back to the historical figure of Sandino, and along with two other people, one of whom was believed to be Casimiro Sotelo, who was later assassinated, founded the [Sandinista National Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandinista_National_Liberation_Front "Sandinista National Liberation Front") (FSLN).[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-SY-92) After the 1972 earthquake and Somoza's apparent corruption, the ranks of the Sandinistas were flooded with young disaffected Nicaraguans who no longer had anything to lose.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Grinnell2007-109)

On December 27, 1974, a group of the FSLN, in an attempt to kidnap U.S. ambassador Turner Shelton, held some Managuan partygoers hostage after killing the party's host, former agriculture minister Jose Maria Castillo, until the Somoza government met their demands for a large ransom and free transport to [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba"). Somoza granted the demand, and then subsequently sent his national guard out into the countryside to look for the kidnappers, who were described by opponents as terrorists.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-110)

On 10 January 1978, [Pedro Joaquín Chamorro Cardenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_Joaqu%C3%ADn_Chamorro_Cardenal "Pedro Joaquín Chamorro Cardenal"), the editor of the national newspaper _[La Prensa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Prensa\_(Managua) "La Prensa (Managua)")_ and ardent opponent of Somoza, was assassinated.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-AC-111) It is alleged that the planners and perpetrators of the murder were at the highest echelons of the Somoza regime.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-AC-111)

The Sandinistas forcefully took power in July 1979, ousting Somoza, and prompting the exodus of the majority of Nicaragua's middle class, wealthy landowners, and professionals, many of whom settled in the United States.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-112)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-113)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-114) The Carter administration decided to work with the new government, while attaching a provision for aid forfeiture if it was found to be assisting insurgencies in neighboring countries.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-115) Somoza fled the country, and eventually ended up in [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay"), where he was assassinated in September 1980, allegedly by members of the Argentinian Revolutionary Workers' Party.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-116)

In 1980, the [Carter administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Jimmy_Carter "Presidency of Jimmy Carter") provided $60 million in aid to Nicaragua under the Sandinistas, but the aid was suspended when the administration obtained evidence of Nicaraguan shipment of arms to El Salvadoran rebels.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-117)Most people sided with Nicaragua against the Sandinistas.[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_][[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-118)

#### Contras (1981–1990)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Contras (1981–1990)")]

Main article: [Contras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contras "Contras")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Contra_commandas_1987.jpg/250px-Contra_commandas_1987.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Contra_commandas_1987.jpg)

A group of [Contras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contras "Contras") in the former [Zelaya Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zelaya_Department "Zelaya Department") on Nicaragua's west coast on the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea"). Women [commonly joined](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role_of_women_in_the_Nicaraguan_Revolution "Role of women in the Nicaraguan Revolution") the Contras as combatants.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-119)

In response to the Sandinistas, various rebel groups collectively known as the "[Contras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contras "Contras")" were formed to oppose the new government. The [Reagan administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Ronald_Reagan "Presidency of Ronald Reagan") ultimately authorized the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") to [help the Contra rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_and_state-sponsored_terrorism#Nicaragua "United States and state-sponsored terrorism") with funding, weapons, and training.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-CA-120) The Contras operated from camps in the neighboring countries of Honduras to the north and Costa Rica to the south.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-CA-120)

They engaged in a systematic campaign of terror among rural Nicaraguans to disrupt the social reform projects of the Sandinistas. Several historians have criticized the Contra campaign and the [Reagan administration's support for the Contras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_Ronald_Reagan_administration "Foreign policy of the Ronald Reagan administration"), citing the brutality and numerous human rights violations of the Contras, alleging that health centers, schools, and cooperatives were destroyed by rebels,[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-121) and that murder, rape, and torture occurred on a large scale in Contra-dominated areas.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-122) The U.S. also carried out a campaign of economic sabotage, and disrupted shipping by planting underwater mines in Nicaragua's port of [Corinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinto,_Nicaragua "Corinto, Nicaragua"),[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-123) an action [condemned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_v._United_States "Nicaragua v. United States") by the [International Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice "International Court of Justice") as illegal.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-124) The court also found that the U.S. encouraged acts contrary to humanitarian law by producing the manual _[Psychological Operations in Guerrilla Warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological\_Operations\_in\_Guerrilla\_Warfare "Psychological Operations in Guerrilla Warfare")_ and disseminating it to the Contras.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-125) The manual, among other things, advised on how to rationalize killings of civilians.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-ReferenceC-126) The U.S. also sought to place economic pressure on the Sandinistas, and the Reagan administration imposed a full trade embargo.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-127)

The Sandinistas were also accused of human rights abuses including torture, disappearances and mass executions.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-128)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-129) The [Inter-American Commission on Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-American_Commission_on_Human_Rights "Inter-American Commission on Human Rights") investigated abuses by Sandinista forces, including an execution of 35 to 40 [Miskitos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miskito_people "Miskito people") in December 1981,[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-130) and an execution of 75 people in November 1984.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-131)

In the [Nicaraguan general elections of 1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaraguan_general_election,_1984 "Nicaraguan general election, 1984"), which were judged by at least one visiting 30-person delegation of NGO representatives to have been free and fair,[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-132) the Sandinistas won the parliamentary election and their leader [Daniel Ortega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Ortega "Daniel Ortega") won the presidential election.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-133) The Reagan administration criticized the elections as a "sham" based on the claim that [Arturo Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Cruz "Arturo Cruz"), the candidate nominated by the [Coordinadora Democrática Nicaragüense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coordinadora_Democr%C3%A1tica_Nicarag%C3%BCense "Coordinadora Democrática Nicaragüense"), comprising three right wing political parties, did not participate in the elections. However, the administration privately argued against Cruz's participation for fear that his involvement would legitimize the elections, and thus weaken the case for American aid to the Contras.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-134)

In 1983 the U.S. Congress prohibited federal funding of the Contras, but the Reagan administration illegally continued to back them by covertly selling arms to [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran") and channeling the proceeds to the Contras in the [Iran–Contra affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Contra_affair "Iran–Contra affair"), for which several members of the Reagan administration were convicted of felonies.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-135) The [International Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice "International Court of Justice"), in regard to the case of [Nicaragua v. United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua_v._United_States "Nicaragua v. United States") in 1986, found, "the United States of America was under an obligation to make reparation to the Republic of Nicaragua for all injury caused to Nicaragua by certain breaches of obligations under customary international law and treaty-law committed by the United States of America".[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-icj-cij-136) During the war between the Contras and the Sandinistas, 30,000 people were killed.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-137)

### Post-war (1990–2018)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Post-war (1990–2018)")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Violeta_Chamorro_1993.jpg/250px-Violeta_Chamorro_1993.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Violeta_Chamorro_1993.jpg)

In 1990, after the [Contra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contras "Contras") war, [Violeta Chamorro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violeta_Chamorro "Violeta Chamorro") became the first woman president democratically elected in the history of the [Americas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americas "Americas").

[![Image 26](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b3/Mitch-Flooding_in_Managua.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mitch-Flooding_in_Managua.jpg)

Flooding in Lake Managua after [Hurricane Mitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Mitch "Hurricane Mitch") in 1998

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Crowd_fills_street_at_a_May_2018_protest.jpg/250px-Crowd_fills_street_at_a_May_2018_protest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crowd_fills_street_at_a_May_2018_protest.jpg)

[Nicaraguan protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%932020_Nicaraguan_protests "2018–2020 Nicaraguan protests") in May 2018

In the [1990 Nicaraguan general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Nicaraguan_general_election "1990 Nicaraguan general election"), a coalition of anti-Sandinista parties from both the left and right of the political spectrum led by [Violeta Chamorro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violeta_Chamorro "Violeta Chamorro"), the widow of Pedro Joaquín Chamorro Cardenal, defeated the Sandinistas. The defeat shocked the Sandinistas, who had expected to win.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-138)

Exit polls of Nicaraguans reported Chamorro's victory over [Ortega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Ortega "Daniel Ortega") was achieved with a 55% majority.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-139) Chamorro was the first woman president of Nicaragua. Ortega vowed he would govern _desde abajo_ (from below).[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-140) Chamorro came to office with an economy in ruins, primarily because of the financial and social costs of the Contra War with the Sandinista-led government.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-141) In the [1996 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Nicaraguan_general_election "1996 Nicaraguan general election"), Daniel Ortega and the Sandinistas of the FSLN lost again, this time to [Arnoldo Alemán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnoldo_Alem%C3%A1n "Arnoldo Alemán") of the [Constitutional Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutionalist_Liberal_Party_(Nicaragua) "Constitutionalist Liberal Party (Nicaragua)") (PLC).

In [the 2001 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Nicaraguan_general_election "2001 Nicaraguan general election"), the PLC again defeated the FSLN, with Alemán's Vice President [Enrique Bolaños](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Bola%C3%B1os "Enrique Bolaños") succeeding him as president. However, Alemán was convicted and sentenced in 2003 to 20 years in prison for [embezzlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embezzlement "Embezzlement"), [money laundering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_laundering "Money laundering"), and corruption;[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-142) liberal and Sandinista parliament members combined to strip the presidential powers of President Bolaños and his ministers, calling for his resignation and threatening [impeachment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment "Impeachment"). The Sandinistas said they no longer supported Bolaños after U.S. Secretary of State [Colin Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Powell "Colin Powell") told Bolaños to distance from the FSLN.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-143) This "slow motion _coup d'état_" was averted partially by pressure from the Central American presidents, who vowed not to recognize any movement that removed Bolaños; the U.S., the OAS, and the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") also opposed the action.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-144)

Nicaragua briefly participated in the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") in 2004 as part of the [Plus Ultra Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plus_Ultra_Brigade "Plus Ultra Brigade"), a military contingent of mixed personnel.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-AP_2004-04-29-145)

Before [the general elections on 5 November 2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Nicaraguan_general_election "2006 Nicaraguan general election"), the [National Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Assembly_of_Nicaragua "National Assembly of Nicaragua") passed a bill further restricting [abortion in Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_in_Nicaragua "Abortion in Nicaragua").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-146) As a result, Nicaragua is one of five countries in the world where abortion is illegal with no exceptions.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-147)

Legislative and presidential elections took place on 5 November 2006. Ortega returned to the presidency with 37.99% of the vote. This percentage was enough to win the presidency outright, because of a change in electoral law which lowered the percentage requiring a runoff election from 45% to 35% (with a 5% margin of victory).[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-148)[Nicaragua's 2011 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Nicaraguan_general_election "2011 Nicaraguan general election") resulted in the re-election of Ortega, with a landslide 62.46% of the vote. In 2014 the National Assembly approved changes to the constitution allowing Ortega to run for a third successive term.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-149)

In November 2016, [Ortega was elected for his third consecutive term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Nicaraguan_general_election "2016 Nicaraguan general election") (his fourth overall). International monitoring of the elections was initially prohibited, and as a result the validity of the [elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elections_in_Nicaragua "Elections in Nicaragua") has been disputed, but observation by the [OAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_of_American_States "Organization of American States") was announced in October.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-150)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-151) Ortega was reported by Nicaraguan election officials as having received 72% of the vote. However, the [Broad Front for Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Front_for_Democracy "Broad Front for Democracy") (FAD), having promoted boycotts of the elections, claimed that 70% of voters had abstained (while election officials claimed 65.8% participation).[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-152)

In April 2018, [demonstrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%932020_Nicaraguan_protests "2018–2020 Nicaraguan protests") were held to oppose a decree increasing taxes and reducing benefits in the country's pension system. Local independent press organizations documented at least 19 dead and over 100 missing in the ensuing conflict.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-153) A reporter from NPR spoke to protestors who explained that while the initial issue was the pension reforms, the uprisings that spread across the country reflected many grievances about the government's time in office, and that the fight is for President Ortega and his vice president, his wife, to step down.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-154)

24 April 2018 marked the day of the greatest march in opposition of the Sandinista party. On 2 May 2018, university student leaders made a public announcement giving the government seven days to set a date and time for a dialogue that was promised to the people due to the recent events of repression. The students also scheduled another peaceful protest march on that same day. As of May 2018, estimates of the death toll were as high as 63, many of them student protesters, and the wounded totaled more than 400.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-155)

Following a working visit from 17 to 21 May, the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights adopted precautionary measures aimed at protecting members of the student movement and their families after testimonies indicated the majority of them had suffered acts of violence and death threats for their participation.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-156) In the last week of May, thousands who accuse Mr. Ortega and his wife of acting like dictators joined in resuming anti-government rallies after attempted peace talks have remained unresolved.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-157) Open suppression of political dissent and more militarized policing began in April 2018, but the onset of repression was gradual.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-158) On 12 October 2024, Nicaragua broke ties with [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel") in response to the ongoing [Gaza war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war"), condemning Israel's leaders as "fascist" and "[genocidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_genocide "Gaza genocide")".[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-159)

**Nicaragua**,[[e]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-19) officially the **Republic of Nicaragua**,[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-20) is a [country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") in [Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_America "Central America"), comprising 130,370 square kilometers (50,340 sq mi). With a population of 7,097,329 as of 2026,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-21) it is the third-most populous country in Central America after [Guatemala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guatemala "Guatemala") and [Honduras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honduras "Honduras"), and the [largest by area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_North_American_countries_by_area "List of North American countries by area") in all of Central America.

Nicaragua is bordered by Honduras to the north, the [Caribbean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Sea "Caribbean Sea") of the [Atlantic Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") to the east, Costa Rica to the south, and the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") to the west. The country also shares maritime borders with [El Salvador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Salvador "El Salvador") to the west and [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") to the east. Nicaragua's largest city and national capital is [Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managua "Managua"), which is also the [fourth-largest city in Central America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_cities_in_Central_America#Largest_cities_proper "List of largest cities in Central America"), with a population of 1,055,247 as of December 2020. Nicaragua is known as "the breadbasket of Central America" due to having the most fertile soil and arable land in all of Central America.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-22)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-23) The official language is [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"), though different groups on the Caribbean coast ([Mosquitia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_Coast "Mosquito Coast")) speak their own languages and [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"). The mixture of cultural traditions has generated substantial diversity in folklore, cuisine, music, and literature, including contributions by Nicaraguan poets and writers such as [Rubén Darío](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rub%C3%A9n_Dar%C3%ADo "Rubén Darío").

Originally inhabited by various indigenous cultures since ancient times, the region was conquered by the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") in the 16th century. Nicaragua gained independence from Spain in 1821. The Caribbean region ([Mosquitia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito_Coast "Mosquito Coast")) followed a different historical path, being an independent kingdom under British protection from the 17th century until 1860 with the signing of the [Treaty of Managua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Managua "Treaty of Managua"), which brought it into a [union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_union "Real union") with Nicaragua, while its northernmost part was placed under Honduras by the Wyke-Cruz Treaty of 1859.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-24) Since its independence, Nicaragua has undergone periods of political unrest, dictatorship, [American occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_occupation_of_Nicaragua "United States occupation of Nicaragua") and fiscal crisis, as well as the [Nicaraguan Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaraguan_Revolution "Nicaraguan Revolution") of the 1960s and 1970s and the [Contra War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contras "Contras") of the 1980s.

Though nominally a unitary presidential republic, Nicaragua has experienced significant [democratic backsliding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_backsliding "Democratic backsliding") since 2007 under the presidency of [Daniel Ortega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Ortega "Daniel Ortega"), resulting in [large protests in 2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Nicaraguan_protests "2018 Nicaraguan protests") and a subsequent crackdown. Following the [2021 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Nicaraguan_general_election "2021 Nicaraguan general election"), it has been widely described as an [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism")[dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictatorship "Dictatorship"),[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-25)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-26)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-27) and the [next national elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_Nicaraguan_general_election "Next Nicaraguan general election") were effectively canceled in 2026.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-28)[_[not verified in body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] It is a developing country and has the [second lowest GDP per capita (nominal)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_American_and_Caribbean_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of Latin American and Caribbean countries by GDP (nominal)") and [fourth lowest GDP per capita (PPP)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_American_and_Caribbean_countries_by_GDP_(PPP) "List of Latin American and Caribbean countries by GDP (PPP)") among Latin American and Caribbean countries. In 2025, Nicaragua was ranked as the second-most corrupt country in Latin America, after [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela "Venezuela"), by the [Corruption Perceptions Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_Perceptions_Index#2020%E2%80%932024 "Corruption Perceptions Index"). Nicaragua's multiethnic population includes people of [mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mestizo "Mestizo"), indigenous, European, and African heritage.

Known as the "land of lakes and volcanoes",[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Brierley-29)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Wallace-30) Nicaragua is also home to the [Bosawás Biosphere Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosaw%C3%A1s_Biosphere_Reserve "Bosawás Biosphere Reserve"), the second-largest tropical rainforest of the Americas.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-31) The biological diversity, warm tropical climate and active volcanoes have made Nicaragua an increasingly popular [tourist destination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourist_destination "Tourist destination").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-32)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-33) Nicaragua is a founding member of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations")[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-34) and is also a member of the [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement"),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-35)[Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivarian_Alliance_for_the_Peoples_of_Our_America "Bolivarian Alliance for the Peoples of Our America"),[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-36) and [Community of Latin American and Caribbean States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_of_Latin_American_and_Caribbean_States "Community of Latin American and Caribbean States").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-37)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nicaragua&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/Gran_Nicoya.jpg/250px-Gran_Nicoya.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gran_Nicoya.jpg)

Location of _Nicanahuac_, the Indigenous name for _[Gran Nicoya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran\_Nicoya?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gran Nicoya (page does not exist)")[[es](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran%20Nicoya "es:Gran Nicoya")]_, an area in western Nicaragua and northwestern Costa Rica inhabited by the Nahuas

The etymology of Nicaragua is _Nicānāhuac_, which was the name the [Nicaraos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicarao_people "Nicarao people"), a [Nawat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nawat "Nawat")-speaking people, gave to the [Greater Nicoya](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gran%20Nicoya "es:Gran Nicoya") region of Nicaragua and Costa Rica.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-38)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-39)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-cclec.org-40)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-41)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-42)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-43)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-44) It means "here lies Anahuac" in Nahuatl and is a combination of the words "nican" (here),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-45) and "[Ānāhuac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anahuac_(Aztec) "Anahuac (Aztec)")", which is a combination of the words "atl" (water) and "nahuac", a locative meaning "surrounded". Therefore, the literal translation of _Nicanahuac_ is "here surrounded by water", which corraborates the theory that the etymology refers to the large bodies of water in and around the country, the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean"), lakes [Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua "Lake Nicaragua") and [Xolotlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Xolotlan "Lake Xolotlan"), and the rivers and lagoons. The name evolved through phonetic changes such as the "n" becoming an _r_ and the _ahuac_ in "anahuac" becoming _agua_ as both "anahuac" and "agua" relate to the concept of water, which would have made it a convenient circumstance for the Spanish in renaming _Nicanahuac_ to _Nicaragua_.

Previous theories about the country's name came from the following: _nican-nahua_, which means "here are the Nahuas"; and [nicarao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicarao_(cacique) "Nicarao (cacique)")-agua. However, in 2002, it was discovered that the real name of the cacique was Macuilmiquiztli and not Nicarao, ultimately debunking this theory.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-46)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-47)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-48)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-49)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-cclec.org-40)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Ideal-50)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Pueblo-51)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-Choque-52)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicaragua#cite_note-53)
